analysis.pattern_summary: Alexandra consistently loses points on sentence-level construction and on following the exact transformation the prompt asks for. She changes meaning or ignores the directive (Q1 "gently teared" instead of a stronger verb for "looked," the "since" combine written with "then," the question rewrite changed to "Why do…get sold," a fragment fixed by adding "She broke"). She also produces run-ons and comma splices (G3.3 Q4, G3.5 Q4), makes subject-verb, tense and spelling errors, and gives short, undeveloped opinion or character responses with no "because" reasoning (G3.4 Q6, Q7, Q8, Q10). Appositive and combining tasks stay weak across tests (G3.3 Q3, G3.5 Q4 scored 0%), and the paragraph tasks are relatively stronger but still have mechanical errors. Scores of 67-80% over four rushed attempts suggest she is close, but the same sentence-level errors keep her below the threshold.
analysis.skill_gaps: appositive phrases, combining sentences with subordinating conjunctions (since/because), run-on and comma splice correction, following transformation directions while preserving meaning, strong verb choice, converting statements to questions (verb inversion), fragment-to-sentence revision, subject-verb agreement and verb tense, explaining reasons (claim plus "because" elaboration), proofreading/spelling, character-trait inference with evidence
analysis.alphawrite_vs_test: AlphaWrite shows MASTERED for Basic Conjunctions, Change Sentence To Question, and Fragment Or Sentence, yet she misses these same skills on tests (the "since" combine, the question rewrite, and the fragment revision). analysis.pattern_summary: Ansel repeatedly misses the targeted transformation tasks. He writes comma-spliced or "and"-joined sentences instead of true appositives (G3.1 Q1, G3.5 Q4), skips the requested conjunction (G3.1 Q4 gave "and the reason might be"; G3.2 Q2 used "then"), and cannot reliably turn a statement into an interrogative (G3.1 Q2 and G3.4 Q3, where he wrote an imperative). He also leaves answers incomplete or off-prompt: fragments (G3.4 Q5), unfinished sentences (G3.1 Q9), a missing "why" (G3.1 Q10), and unsupported claims (G3.2 Q5). Paragraph responses (Q11) are inconsistent: he scored 65%, 50%, and 80% when he wrote, but 0% on the last two, which were blank. Frequent run-ons, spelling and punctuation errors, and blank or rushed late-test responses keep his scores in the 50-78% range.
analysis.skill_gaps: appositive construction, combining sentences with a specified conjunction (because/but/so), converting statements to interrogatives, sentence types (a blank answer on declarative/interrogative identification), complete sentences vs. fragments, run-ons and comma splices, subject-verb agreement, answering all parts of a prompt (explain why), text-evidence integration and explaining the "so what" in paragraphs, conventions (spelling, capitalization, apostrophes), stamina and completion on paragraph-length responses
analysis.alphawrite_vs_test: Ansel shows every Sentences G3 and Paragraphs G3 skill as MASTERED, including Combine Sentences, Write Appositives, and Combine Sentences With Appositives, with only 1 attempt each and no recorded scores. Yet he still fails appositive, conjunction, and question-transformation items on the tests, so the AlphaWrite mastery isn't transferring to independent written responses. The single attempts and missing scores suggest the mastery flags may reflect shallow practice.
analysis.rushing_impact: Rushing probably had a moderate effect: G3.2 and G3.5 were both rushed, with a blank answer on G3.2 Q4 and a blank paragraph on G3.5 Q11 (a 0% that alone pulled the score down about 10-15 points), though his errors on non-rushed tests (G3.1, G3.4) show the underlying skill gaps are real.
analysis.recommended_activities:
- Combine Sentences With Appositives (Sentences G3): redo with a high accuracy threshold and multiple attempts, since he writes comma splices or "and" clauses instead of true appositives.
- Write Appositives (Sentences G3): practice identifying the noun and adding a renaming phrase set off by commas, e.g. "My family owns two dogs, Lucy and Rocket."
- Combine Sentences (Sentences G3): drill because/but/so, including following the specific conjunction named in the prompt.
- Write Sentence From Prompt (Sentences G3): practice statement-to-question rewrites and sentence-type identification (declarative/interrogative/imperative/exclamatory), plus complete sentences vs. fragments.
- Elaborate Paragraphs (Paragraphs G3), plus a Writing Brainlift on paragraph structure and text evidence: practice topic sentence, two text details, and explanation, along with a pre-submit checklist (answer every part, no blank responses, proofread for run-ons and spelling).

analysis.pattern_summary: Austin's errors are mostly in mechanics and in depth of text-based support. He drops end punctuation (no question mark on the rewritten question) and misplaces commas (a comma after "since"), and he makes spelling and word-choice slips ("apon"). On the paragraph prompts (Q11 on both tests, 55% and 65%), his answers stay general. They lack specific article details and text evidence, and the explanation stops short of what the prompt asks. On G3.2 Q6 he also gave an inference that was off target (the team's name rather than helping children and having fun), which suggests shaky comprehension or inference from the text.
analysis.skill_gaps: end punctuation for question sentences, comma use with subordinating conjunctions, proofreading and editing, spelling and word choice, paragraph development, text evidence integration, specific supporting details, inference from informational text, completing the full task in extended responses
analysis.alphawrite_vs_test: Austin shows mastery on Combine Sentences, Appositives, and Topic Brainstorm in AlphaWrite, yet he still makes errors on test sentence combining (the comma after "since") and writes underdeveloped paragraphs. This suggests the skills hold up in isolated, scaffolded practice but not under independent, timed conditions, where he lacks a proofreading habit and the stamina to add detail. The quiz scores are also missing (None%) with only one attempt each, so the "mastered" status is weakly supported.
analysis.rushing_impact: The G3.2 test (73%) was flagged as rushed and likely cost him points on careless errors like the missing question mark and thin details; the G3.4 test was not rushed and still showed the same paragraph weaknesses, so rushing was a contributing factor but not the root cause.
analysis.recommended_activities:
- Combine Sentences With Subordinating Conjunctions (Sentences G3): the comma error with "since" shows he needs practice with when a comma is and isn't needed in complex sentences, and the earlier mastery came from only one attempt.
- Paragraphs G3 > Supporting Details / Evidence from Text (Paragraphs G3): his Q11 responses lack specific article details, so he needs practice selecting and citing concrete facts.
- Paragraph Drafting and Elaboration (Paragraphs G3): he needs to build full paragraphs with a topic sentence, 2-3 detailed supports, and a concluding sentence, rather than stopping at general claims.
- Revise and Edit / Proofreading Checklist (Sentences G3): this builds a habit of checking end punctuation, commas, and spelling before submitting, which addresses the missing question mark, comma error, and "apon."
- Writing Brainlift: Re-read the Prompt and Plan Before Writing: he should practice annotating the prompt and article, identifying the main reason or key idea (as in the Teddy Bear Toss question), and planning evidence before writing, which also counters rushing.

analysis.pattern_summary: Austin's scores (78%, 60%, 80%, 48%, 44%) swing widely because of persistent weaknesses in sentence-combining and restructuring tasks (appositives, "because" clauses, question formation, conjunction use) and in the Q11 extended paragraph. Those paragraphs are often thin (35%), or blank (0% on G3.6 and G3.7). He also makes recurring convention errors: missing end punctuation, lowercase names ("layla," "jason"), misspellings ("swa," "string," "anamal"), run-ons and comma splices, and sentence fragments ("Because they are used to no water"). He often answers the prompt but skips the reason or evidence the prompt requires, for example the "why is it important" part of G3.4 Q10 and the "warm soil" reason in G3.7 Q6. The last two tests show a clear decline in effort and stamina, and the 0% blank paragraphs suggest disengagement or time pressure rather than only a skill deficit.
analysis.skill_gaps: appositive phrases, combining sentences while keeping both subjects and ideas, "because"/subordinating conjunction clause construction, question formation (helping verbs, question marks), complete sentences vs. fragments, comma usage and run-on control, capitalization of proper nouns, proofreading and spelling, paragraph development with text evidence, supporting a claim with a reason, writing stamina and task initiation
analysis.alphawrite_vs_test: Austin has mastered nearly every G3 AlphaWrite activity, including Combine Sentences, Basic Conjunctions, Write Paragraph From Prompt, and Write Freeform Paragraph, yet he still fails the same skills on tests (appositives, "because" combinations, paragraph writing). Mastery with scaffolding does not transfer to independent, timed, text-based writing, and the mastered activities show no scores, so passing them may not reflect real proficiency. His lapses in proofreading and effort on tests also don't appear in AlphaWrite.
analysis.rushing_impact: G3.7 was flagged as rushed and ended with a blank paragraph (0%) and a skipped feedback item, so rushing probably contributed substantially to the 44%, though G3.6 (48%) was also weak and blank without being flagged, which suggests skill and engagement problems beyond rushing.
analysis.recommended_activities:
- Combine Sentences Using Appositives (Sentences G3): he missed the appositive items on G3.5 Q4 and G3.6 Q3 and wrote run-on additions instead of embedded descriptive phrases.
- Combining with Subordinating Conjunctions: because, since, although (Combining G3): "because" and "since" combinations were inconsistent, with comma splices and unclear cause-and-effect.
- Write Paragraph From Prompt, repeated with text evidence (Paragraphs G3): the Q11 paragraphs lack text details and two were left blank. Redo it under timed, independent conditions with a required evidence sentence.
- Turn Outline Into Draft (Paragraphs G3): practice planning a brief outline (topic sentence, two details, conclusion) before writing, so he can start the paragraph instead of leaving it empty.
- Sentence Types and End Punctuation / Proofreading Checklist (Writing Brainlift): targets missing question marks, capitalized names, fragments, and spelling errors that cost points in nearly every test.

The holes had caught the water and the compost had given the plants nutrients. Today greenery grows where a desert once was. Now Yacouba visits other villages and other people and teaches them how to bring life back to a desert. And all over West Africa people make zaï holes along with other ways to save water. And it's all because of Yacouba!
questions.feedback: “The holes had caught the water and the compost had given the plants nutrients” clearly explains how Yacouba’s method worked, using strong details from the article. For example: “Yacouba’s smart idea for zaï holes and his belief in his plan helped plants grow even when the land was dry.” Your ending nicely shows that his idea helped people across West Africa.

analysis.pattern_summary: Across all three tests, Aya repeatedly writes comma splices and run-ons, joining two complete thoughts with only a comma (G4.1 Q1, Q10; G4.2 Q5, Q9, Q10; G4.3 Q9). Her ideas and content are usually strong, so the gap is in sentence-boundary control, not idea generation. She also has trouble with precise task execution: she writes fragments that lack a main verb (G4.3 Q5), misorders words (G4.3 Q2), puts the appositive on the wrong noun (G4.2 Q4), and misplaces or adds commas before subordinate clauses (G4.1 Q4). Scores fell from 86% to 78% to 71%, which suggests the same unresolved errors recur, and in G4.3 the short, targeted sentence-level items dropped to 0%.
analysis.skill_gaps: comma splices/run-on correction, sentence boundary punctuation, fragment-to-complete-sentence repair (adding a main verb), word order/syntax revision, appositive targeting (describing the correct noun), comma use with subordinate clauses, combining sentences with logical clause order, answering the specific prompt (staying on task), topic-sentence framing in paragraphs, preserving original wording and meaning when revising
analysis.alphawrite_vs_test: Aya has mastered every G4 skill in AlphaWrite (conjunctions, combining, appositives, fragments, subordinating conjunctions, paragraphs), yet she still fails the same skills on tests. The quizzes likely check recognition or guided practice, not independent, self-edited writing, and the mastery came after only 1-3 attempts, so it may not have been consolidated. The "best" and "latest" percentages are also missing (None%), so mastery here can't be checked against actual scores.
analysis.rushing_impact: The G4.2 rush probably caused a moderate drop (the 78% shows run-ons and a missed appositive target that careful proofreading could have caught), but the lower, unrushed G4.3 score of 71% shows that rushing is not the main cause.
analysis.recommended_activities:
- Fix Run-Ons and Comma Splices (Sentences G4/G5): comma splices appear in nearly every long-response answer, and she needs explicit practice splitting or joining with a conjunction or semicolon.
- Fragment Or Sentence, then Expand Fragments (Sentences G4 / To Sentence G4): she wrote "Nearby, a caterpillar who…" without a main verb, so she needs to practice finding the missing predicate and rewriting.
- Write Appositives / Combine Sentences With Appositives (Production G4): in G4.2 Q4 she described the wrong noun, so she should practice targeting the appositive to the noun named in the prompt.
- Subordinating Conjunctions (Sentences G4): she adds an unneeded comma before "if" and misorders cause and effect in "because" sentences, so she needs practice with clause order and comma rules.
- Write Paragraph From Prompt with a self-edit checklist (Writing Brainlift): the checklist (topic sentence stating the prompt, one comma check per sentence, "does each sentence answer the question?") would address her off-task and long-sentence habits. Pair it with a Writing Brainlift revision activity where she proofreads her own sentences before submitting.

analysis.pattern_summary: Brooke scores 80-87% overall, but she repeatedly loses points on the 50% sentence-level tasks that require following a specific structural instruction. She wrote an appositive with broken punctuation (G3.1), added extra clauses instead of making a sentence concise (G3.2), left out the appositive entirely (G3.3), and used "so" instead of the required "since" (G3.4). Her one-sentence responses also tend to answer only part of the prompt. She gave no action in the dog-barking question, no reason in the "rule for natural places" question, and no character trait explained by Layla's actions. Her paragraphs have good ideas but are held back by conventions: spelling errors (famliy, suprised, humas, thier), run-on or comma-spliced sentences, missing capitals, and homophone errors (there/their, then/than). Q5 in G3.3 earned 0% on a word-choice item, apparently because she rewrote the whole sentence instead of supplying one word.
analysis.skill_gaps: following precise task directions (required conjunction/appositive/one-sentence limits), appositive construction and punctuation, subordinating conjunction use (since/because), concise sentence revision (removing redundancy), run-on and comma-splice correction, answering all parts of a prompt (action, reason, explanation), capitalization and proofreading, spelling and homophones, sentence boundaries within paragraphs, supporting claims with explanation ("why it matters")
analysis.alphawrite_vs_test: Brooke has mastered nearly every G3 skill in AlphaWrite, including appositives, subordinating conjunctions, combining sentences, fragments and sentences, and paragraph writing, yet she still misses these same skills on the tests (appositive in G3.3, "since" in G3.4). This suggests a transfer gap: she can do the skills in scaffolded, isolated practice but does not apply them reliably in open-ended written responses, where she does not check her work against the prompt's requirements or proofread.
analysis.rushing_impact: The G3.4 test was flagged as rushed, and the "so" for "since" substitution and the very short, incomplete answers on Q6 and Q10 likely cost her points, but her score (84%) is in line with her other attempts, so rushing was probably a minor factor rather than the main cause of the loop.
analysis.recommended_activities:

analysis.pattern_summary: Brooks's weak points are on short constructed-response items: he doesn't elaborate or support his answers, and he doesn't follow the exact transformation the prompt asks for. He often gives fragments or bare answers ("Because it's more fun," "Yes I do"), and he restates a statement instead of changing its sentence type (G3.2 Q3 and G3.4 Q3 both missed). On the culminating paragraph prompts (Q11 on G3.5, G3.6, G3.7, and G3.8), which are the highest-weight tasks, he answered with refusals or off-topic text ("im goood dude no thanks", "HHEEEEECCCKKK NAAAAHHHHHH", "......really bruh...."). Scores fell from 44% to 49% to 22% to 33%. His responses became less effortful over time, even though he showed capability when he engaged (67% on several items).
analysis.skill_gaps: appositive phrase construction (not substituting conjunctions), writing complete sentences with a reason (because/explanation), capitalization and spelling conventions, text-evidence integration from passages, one-paragraph response development (topic sentence, details, conclusion), answering the specific question asked, sustained effort and engagement on extended writing
analysis.alphawrite_vs_test: Carter has mastered every AlphaWrite skill listed, including both appositive quizzes and Write Freeform Paragraph, yet he still fails appositive items and paragraph prompts on tests. analysis.pattern_summary: Conan's responses are generally on topic and understandable, but they are consistently underdeveloped and mechanically unpolished. On G3.1 he runs sentences together with comma splices and omits spaces, capitals, and end punctuation. He also gives fragments or bare answers (e.g., "Tell the owner...") that lack a reason or text evidence, which is what the prompts ask for. On G3.4 the same problems recur: he writes a question with a period, gives one-clause answers with no supporting detail ("Layla loves nature."), misreads the text (nature led her to keep the geode, not do the right thing), and organizes the paragraph as a run-on list with comma errors. His scores of 43% and 62% show that low-level sentence construction and elaboration are the barrier, not comprehension of the topic.
analysis.skill_gaps: appositive/sentence combining, end punctuation and capitalization, comma usage and comma splices, run-on and fragment correction, complete-sentence responses, elaboration with reasons ("because" statements), text evidence integration, accurate text comprehension of character and theme, interrogative sentence conversion, paragraph structure (topic sentence, transitions, closing), proofreading and editing
analysis.alphawrite_vs_test: Conan is marked mastered on Identify Appositives, Write Freeform Paragraph, and Write Paragraph From Prompt, yet he still failed to form an appositive on G3.1 Q1 and wrote a run-on, list-like paragraph on G3.4 Q11. This suggests his mastery is recognition-level or low-bar (all with 1–2 attempts and no recorded scores), and does not transfer to producing and editing his own writing under test conditions.
analysis.rushing_impact: The G3.4 test was flagged as rushed, and the missing end punctuation, terse one-clause answers, and unfinished paragraph likely cost him some points, but the same errors appeared on the unrushed G3.1 test, so rushing is an aggravating factor rather than the root cause.
analysis.recommended_activities:
- Combine Sentences Using Appositives (Sentences G3): he could identify appositives but could not write one when combining sentences on G3.1 Q1, so he needs production practice.
- Fix Run-On Sentences and Comma Splices (Sentences G3): his comma-joined clauses ("...dogs,Their names...", "...pets ,this rule...") appear on multiple items.
- Sentence Types and End Punctuation: Statements, Questions, Commands (Sentences G3): he wrote an interrogative with a period and often omitted capitals and periods.
- Expand Sentences with Because/Reasons (Sentences G3): his answers on G3.1 Q6–Q8 and G3.4 Q6 and Q8 give a claim but no reason or detail.
- Write Paragraph with Topic Sentence, Details, and Conclusion (Paragraphs G3): his G3.4 Q11 response is a single run-on sequence, and he needs to practice structured paragraphs with transitions and complete sentences, with a proofreading checklist before submitting.

questions.title: Extended text (written response)
questions.prompt:
Write an **expository essay** explaining how the solar panel project improved life in the village.

Use information from the passage to describe at least three different ways the project changed the community. Organize your ideas clearly and support them with details from the text.

**Make sure your response includes the following**:

**Write 5 clear paragraphs**: Introduction with a strong thesis, 3 body paragraphs with topic sentences, and a conclusion (5 points)

**Use evidence and explain it
questions.student_answer:
In the village, the solar panel project improved life in the village from having to use candles to having actual lights and solar panels.

There are many reasons why the solar panels made people's life in the village easier. First, the solar panels improved life in the village because when there were no solar panels, the children were unable to do their homework in the dark. When the solar panels became a thing in the village the children were now able to do their homework in the dark. Second, the shops would close later, so people can do more shopping because there is enough light in the store to shop. Third, the small medical clinic, which once closed at sunset, could store vaccines and operate equipment at night and stay open later.

The solar panels changed many peoples lives. One way how it changed many peoples lives is when people need to stay up later to do work around the house, they used to have to stop their work at sunset because they couldn't see what they were doing in the dark, solar panels fixed that. Another way it changed peoples lives was that it strengthened the spirit of cooperation among neighbors.

The people in the village were happy because their lives improved a lot. They now can spend the evenings in laughter and conversation in the streets at night with light a reminder of how progress can bring people together.

The people in the village were very grateful for the new solar panels so that their lives can b e improved.
questions.feedback: You use several accurate details from the passage, including children studying at night, shops staying open later, and the clinic storing vaccines. Your opening clearly states that solar panels replaced candles with electric light, and you also notice that neighbors became more cooperative. To strengthen your essay, explain more fully why each example improved the village instead of moving quickly from one effect to the next. For example, after mentioning the clinic, you could write, “Because the clinic could keep vaccines cold and use equipment at night, villagers could receive safer medical care when they needed it.” Keep building each body paragraph around one main benefit so your explanations can be more detailed.

analysis.pattern_summary: Cruz repeatedly misses the same sentence-level items: identifying sentence type (marked "Imperative" for a declarative sentence on both G7.1 and G7.2), choosing the sentence that doesn't belong or best supports a topic (G7.2 Q7, Q9; G7.3 Q7), and combining ideas logically (G7.3 Q3). Every extended essay scored a flat 70% (G7.4's 80% is the overall score), and the grader feedback is consistent: accurate details are listed but not explained, so elaboration and analysis of evidence are weak. Spelling errors ("nescessity," "enviornment," "benifit," "taht") and a formulaic First/Second/Third structure suggest limited editing and shallow paragraph development, which keeps the overall scores at 70-80%, short of the threshold needed to advance.
analysis.skill_gaps: sentence type identification (declarative vs. imperative), paragraph relevance/cohesion (spotting off-topic sentences), selecting supporting evidence for a topic sentence, logical sentence combining (cause/effect, subordination), elaboration and explanation of evidence, essay analysis beyond listing details, proofreading/spelling
analysis.alphawrite_vs_test: Cruz is marked MASTERED on Identify Sentence Type, Change Sentence Type, Combine Sentences, and Basic Conjunctions, yet misses the same question types on tests (sentence type twice, combining once). Essays G7 > Identify is the only essay stage not mastered, and the other essay stages (Outline, Draft, Polish) show 5 attempts each with mastery, so the tests suggest the skills aren't transferring or being retained. This points to a disconnect between completing AlphaWrite activities and applying the skills under test conditions, especially for evidence selection and elaboration.
analysis.rushing_impact: No timing or rushing data is provided, so the impact can't be determined. The repeated identical errors, such as the same wrong "Imperative" answer on G7.1 and G7.2, suggest a conceptual gap or careless pattern rather than just rushing.
analysis.recommended_activities:
- Identify Sentence Type (Sentences G7): Cruz answered "Imperative" for declarative sentences on two tests, so he needs targeted review and spaced practice with a mastery check, not just completion.
- Essays G7 > Identify (Essays G7): this is the only essay stage not mastered, and it likely trains finding relevant evidence and main ideas, which maps to the Q7/Q9 "does not belong" and "best supports" misses.
- Combine Sentences / Combining G7 Combine Sentences Quiz (Sentences G7): redo with emphasis on logical relationships (cause/effect, contrast) since Cruz chose a simple "and" combination on G7.3 Q3.
- Kernel Expansion (Sentences G7): builds the detail and elaboration needed to explain why evidence matters, which is the recurring essay feedback.
- Essays G7 > Polish (Essays G7): repeat with a focus on proofreading for spelling and on adding explanation sentences after each piece of evidence.

analysis.pattern_summary: Across G3.1 to G3.5 the student gives fragments or very short answers in place of full, developed sentences, and leaves the paragraph prompt (Q11) blank or as filler ("mm", "nhh"). Sentence-combining tasks fail on the same mechanics each time: misplaced commas around conjunctions ("and,", "because,"), no true appositive, dropped nouns, and spelling or capitalization slips. The G3.6 score of 78% shows the student can write a developed paragraph (Q11 at 65%), but he still lets pronoun and noun errors, vague details, and missing reasons through. This suggests that effort and stamina vary from test to test more than the underlying skill does.
analysis.skill_gaps: appositive construction, conjunction use and comma placement, fixing sentence fragments, writing complete sentences with a reason or explanation, elaboration and supporting detail, paragraph stamina and task initiation, proofreading (spelling, capitalization, subject-verb agreement, verb forms), staying on the subject of the prompt (accuracy of noun and detail)
analysis.alphawrite_vs_test: Every AlphaWrite skill is marked MASTERED, including appositives, conjunctions, combining sentences, and paragraph writing, yet the student still fails these exact tasks on tests (G3.1 Q1, G3.5 Q4, and G3.2 Q2 each at 0-50%). This suggests the mastery does not transfer to timed, unscaffolded writing, or that the quizzes were passed with support or in few attempts (many with only 1-2 attempts and no recorded scores).
analysis.rushing_impact: Rushing probably had a large effect on G3.1 and G3.4, where answers were one- to three-word fragments and unedited, and G3.6 was also rushed but still scored 78%, so low effort and engagement appear to matter as much as skill gaps.
analysis.recommended_activities:

analysis.pattern_summary: Davis consistently writes answers that are partly correct but incomplete. He states a claim without a reason or example ("the fans are diehards," "a tradition for the bears," "many things a child can feel"), and he restates the prompt instead of explaining *why* ("The golden spines helped the books stand out"). He also has trouble combining sentences. He picks the wrong conjunction or logic ("because of this" reverses cause and effect, "yet" ignores the because/but/so directions) and uses comma splices ("golden spines, the books also had..."). Frequent spelling, punctuation, and usage errors ("animls," "thier," "popluar," "there/their," "gold spikes") and weakly developed paragraph responses (Q11 on both tests, about 65%) keep his scores in the 70s and him in the loop.
analysis.skill_gaps: elaboration with a reason or example (because/for example), answering the full question (opinion plus reasoning), choosing logical conjunctions (because/but/so) and following the prompt's directions, avoiding comma splices, appositive construction, avoiding redundancy and wordiness in revising, paragraph organization and development with text details, proofreading (spelling, homophones, capitalization, punctuation)
analysis.alphawrite_vs_test: Davis shows Combine Sentences, Write Appositives, Fragment or Sentence, and Unscramble Sentences as mastered at G3, but he still fails conjunction-combining and appositive items on the tests (comma splices, "yet," the reversed "because of this," and an appositive attempt that is really a run-on). The disconnect is that he succeeds on structured, scaffolded items but doesn't transfer the skills to open-ended written responses, where he must follow directions, check logic, and proofread on his own. The mastery data also shows no best/latest scores and only 1 attempt per skill, so it may reflect thin evidence of mastery.
analysis.rushing_impact: The G3.2 test was rushed, and rushing probably contributed to the careless errors and underdeveloped one-line answers (Q5, Q9), but the same patterns appear on the non-rushed G3.5 test (Q6, Q7, Q3), so rushing was likely a minor factor next to the real skill gaps.
analysis.recommended_activities:
- Combine Sentences (Sentences G3), retake at higher rigor with a focus on because/but/so: Davis picks illogical or off-prompt conjunctions and uses comma splices, so he needs to practice matching the conjunction to the relationship between ideas.
- Write Appositives (Sentences G3), repeat with a transfer focus: his test appositive attempt was a comma-spliced run-on, so he needs to practice turning a second sentence into a noun phrase set off by commas.
- Writing Brainlift: Elaboration with "because" or "for example" (Sentences/Paragraphs G3): he gives claims without reasons (Q5, Q6, Q7, Q9), so he needs a routine of claim, then because, then detail.
- Writing Brainlift: Answer the Whole Question (Paragraphs G3): he answers part of the prompt (a tradition vs. "is it a good way to help others?"), so he should practice underlining the question's parts and responding to each.
- Writing Brainlift: Revise and Proofread Checklist (Conventions G3): errors like "animls," "thier," "there/their," and comma splices, plus repetition ("That day... in one day"), call for a self-check on spelling, homophones, punctuation, and redundancy before submitting.

mastered_in_alphawrite_not_tests.skill: Identify Topic Sentence And Sequence Details

analysis.pattern_summary: Donovan repeatedly loses points on sentence-transformation items that require following a precise instruction. These include rewriting a statement as a question (0% on G3.1 Q2 and G3.4 Q3, and 50% on G3.5 Q1 for a missing "?"), combining sentences with an appositive (50% on G3.1 Q1 and G3.5 Q4, 0% on G3.5 Q5 where he answered only "The"), and swapping in a stronger verb (G3.4 Q1). He often writes a correct but different sentence instead of the requested structure, for example restating the sentence, adding "because," or using words that weren't given. He also has recurring convention slips: missing or wrong end punctuation, capitalization, and spelling ("pla," "souvenier," "Caribian"). His short responses (Q7–Q10) stay at about 33–67% because he gives no reason or elaboration. His paragraph scores rose from 40% to 80%, so paragraph writing is no longer the main barrier.
analysis.skill_gaps: appositive construction and identification, converting statements to interrogatives (word order plus "?"), following the exact task instruction (using only given words, changing the verb rather than adding a phrase), end punctuation and capitalization, spelling and proofreading, elaborating with reasons (because/so), stronger verb choice, staying on the prompt in short constructed responses
analysis.alphawrite_vs_test: Donovan has mastered Sentences G3 skills (Identify Sentence Type, Write Sentence From Prompt, Unscramble Sentences) and Paragraphs G3 skills in AlphaWrite, yet he still misses the same kinds of items on tests (unscrambling, sentence-type transformation, prompt-specific writing). This suggests mastery isn't transferring to open-ended, constrained-response formats, and AlphaWrite doesn't cover appositives or interrogative transformation at all. The best and latest scores were not recorded, so how solid the mastery is can't be confirmed.
analysis.rushing_impact: No rushing data was provided. Careless errors such as missing question marks, a one-word answer ("The"), and typos suggest some inattention, but the consistent structural misses point to skill gaps rather than rushing.
analysis.recommended_activities:
- Combine Sentences Using Appositives (Sentences G3/G4): he missed appositive combining on G3.1 and G3.5 and could not identify an appositive, so he needs explicit instruction and practice with comma-set-off phrases.
- Identify Sentence Type and Rewrite Statements as Questions (Sentences G3): he scored 0–50% on interrogative rewrites, so he needs practice with inversion ("Did the geode feel…?", "Were the books sold…?") and ending with "?".
- Write Sentence From Prompt with Constraints (Sentences G3): this builds the habit of using only the given words or the requested structure, which addresses the unscramble and "change the verb" misses.
- Elaborate

questions.title: Extended text (written response)
questions.prompt:
Write an **expository essay** explaining how students learn new languages in effective ways.

Use information from the passage to support your ideas.

**Make sure your response includes the following**:

**Write 5 clear paragraphs**: Introduction with a strong thesis, 3 body paragraphs with topic sentences, and a conclusion (5 points)

**Use evidence and explain it**: Support each point with facts or examples from the passage and explain what they show (5 points)

**Stay organized and on topic**
questions.student_answer: In a busy neighborhood café, people speak many different languages. A family at one table talks in Spanish. At the counter, a worker sings along to a French song on the radio. Scenes like this happen across the United States, a country shaped by immigrants. Even though English is the most common school language, many Americans grow up using two languages at home and in their communities. Learning multiple languages can help people in many different ways. Studies show it can help with memorization and improve resilience and problem-solving skills. Studies also show that infants and younger kids learn faster and have an easier time using proper pronunciation. As a result, many families have started teaching kids second languages while they are infants. One of many ways children can learn is through immersion. Immersion is a class where the teachers use the language during all parts of the day, from simple conversation to learning new subjects. Using the immersion method can help kids hear the language and figure out the vocabulary. One other helpful method uses real communication. Some classrooms connect students with pen pals across the globe. When students reach out to them, they create a bond. This bond can help kids find motivation to learn their language to understand the culture of their pen pal. In conclusion, learning a second language is important for understanding immigrants and peers. Learning a new language can help a child grow their brain and understand others' culture. Languages can be taught in multiple different ways, including immersion and talking to pen pals. Children can also be taught at a young age to make pronunciation easier. Languages have many purposes in a child's brain, but the main reason is to help others share culture and feel welcome.
questions.feedback: You clearly explain several effective ways students can learn languages, including starting young, using immersion, and communicating with pen pals. Your explanation that pen pals can motivate students to practice so they can understand another culture is especially strong. To make your essay easier to follow, separate it into five paragraphs: an introduction with your main claim, one paragraph for each learning method, and a conclusion. This structure will help each important idea stand out and give your reader clear pauses between your points.

questions.student_answer:
For many years, the Mithi River in Mumbai, India, was full of trash. Factories dumped waste into the water. Sewage flowed in every day. The river turned black, and it smelled so bad that people stayed away.

When hope seemed lost, a group called Earth5R showed up. They wanted to return the river to its original beauty. They knew it would take hard work and sacrifice. They also knew they could not do it alone.

First, the group mapped out the river and marked the parts that needed the most cleaning. They took water samples to see where the waste was affecting the river most. Then, they held a volunteer event where anyone could come and help the river flourish. At first, few community members came. But soon, more and more people joined. After a few months, the group had removed over fourteen tonnes of trash.

Over time, the river began to return to its original state. Tests showed the water was twenty percent cleaner than before! Eventually, the community started hanging out near the river again.

The project helped the community grow and flourish. It taught the people that everyone should play their part, and not just let the professionals handle it. Volunteers learned to work together as a community and realize that regular people can take action too. Currently, the community holds cleanups to maintain the river's condition and keep it the same for years.

analysis.pattern_summary: Emma's failures center on the Q11 extended written response (expository essay), where two of three attempts were refusals ("I can not write this essay," "I am not writing this no matter what"). The refusals point to writing avoidance and low self-efficacy more than a pure skill deficit. Her one real attempt (G6.2, 67%) showed an organized structure and text evidence, but the grader noted she copied or closely paraphrased the passage and did not explain why each example matters. The Q11 weights differ across tests (15%, 50%, 10%), so the score swings are driven largely by whether she attempts the essay at all.
analysis.skill_gaps: writing confidence/task initiation, paraphrasing source text in own words, elaborating and explaining evidence (reasoning/commentary), developing a thesis and topic sentence from the prompt, sustained multi-paragraph essay production, persistence on open-ended tasks
analysis.alphawrite_vs_test: Emma has mastered every Essays G6 stage (Outline, Draft, Revise, Polish) plus topic sentence and detail sequencing in AlphaWrite, yet she refuses or underperforms on timed, passage-based essay tests. The disconnect is likely between scaffolded, low-stakes practice and independent, high-stakes test writing, with a confidence and motivation barrier. Mastery with no recorded scores (best/latest = None) also suggests the mastery may reflect completion rather than demonstrated skill.
analysis.rushing_impact: All three tests were rushed, and rushing likely had a major impact: the two refusal responses (43% and 40%) were essentially zero-effort on the essay, and even the 67% attempt lacked the elaboration that more time would have allowed.
analysis.recommended_activities:
- Draft (Essays G6): redo with a passage-based expository prompt under a supervised, low-pressure setup, so she practices turning an outline into full paragraphs with her own wording instead of copying the text.
- Outline (Essays G6): use a thesis, evidence, and explanation planning frame ("This shows... because...") so she has a concrete starting point and no blank page on test day.
- Revise (Essays G6): focus on adding explanation sentences after each piece of text evidence and replacing copied phrases with paraphrase, which is the grader's main feedback.
- Identify Topic Sentence And Sequence Details (Writing Brainlift/Skill Plan): practice writing a strong opening claim directly from a prompt and passage, like the monarch example the grader suggested.
- Timed Low-Stakes Essay Practice (Writing Brainlift): short, untimed-to-timed 10–15 minute passage-response drafts with coach encouragement, to build stamina and reduce avoidance before the next high-stakes test.

First, he cannot do sentence-transformation tasks: he does not write appositives (Q1 on G3.1, Q3 on G3.3), does not combine sentences (Q4 on G3.3, where he left two sentences with a period between them), and does not turn a statement into a question (Q3 on G3.4, where he rewrote it as another statement). **Make sure your response includes the following**:

**Write 5 clear paragraphs**: Intro
questions.student_answer:
Most people believe that self-driving cars will be the future of transportation. They believe this because they will allow people who cannot drive to have the freedom to travel. However, it is important for people to understant both the benefits and the concerns of self-driving cars before they become more common.

First, let's talk about the benefits of new self-driving cars. One benefit is that self-driving cars should stay focused and stop crashes caused by human error. The self-driving aspect of it would allow people who might not be able to drive, like elderly or disabled people, to have the freedom to travel again. Self-driving cars give many benefits to the community.

On the otherhand, many people have concerns about self-driving cars. One concern is what happens if a car fails? In one driving test conducted in Arizona, the car sensed the person but fail to stop in time. One other concern is that many people will lose their jobs. Right now in the USA, millions of people work driving cars and trucks. In summary, tons of people have concerns about self-driving cars, such as that many people will lose their jobs.

There are also some legal questions about self-driving cars. Such as, what happens when a self-driving car gets into a crash? Who would be to blame? The owner? The manufacturer? The software company? Who would the other rider sue? These questions also need to be answered before self-driving cars become more common.

It's important for people to understand the benefits and concerns before making a desision, or explaining the conflict to other people. Self-driving cars, like all new inventions, should always be questioned before becomming common. The benefits and concerns for making any new product or invention are always important for people to understand, so that they can grasp what they are voting for.

questions.student_answer:
Your brain is an amazing tool allowing you to remember tons of different experiences. Your brain take special steps such as remembering a memory that happened many years ago, to self regulating what memories to keep. The brain forms, stores, and retrieves memories and each step effects how you remember experiances.

First, you body collects data from a experiance that is happening in the moment. That data travels to thet brain via nerve cells. The human body contain billions of these cells, and their able to contain thousand more inside of them. there are small gaps between these cells, called synapses, that allow information to pass through them to the next cell. The first step effects how you remember things by taking information into the brain to store it.

Not all information gets saved. Your brain filters out the memories that it thinks aren't inportant, an example being a random moment at school. The part of the brain that filters out this info is called the hippocampus, located in the back of the brain. The hippocampus works during sleep. A test done with students shows that a student that studies right before bed does better on a test than one that stayed up all night. The hippocampus allow the brain to not keep all the information that is not important helping the human to remember important memories.

The way your remember different experiences can change too. When your mood, environment, an even what your thoughts change the way you remember a event changes. A group of divers were tested with a memories game in the water, then after half were tested on land and half in the water. then half that retested in the water remembers more tht the half on land. This is called state dependent memory, when you envrionment changes the way you remember things does to. You mood, environment, and thoughts can change the way you remember an event, causing you the remember it differently.

To summerize, The brain forms, stores, and remembers an event through different steps, and they can change how the event is remembered. An example of this is, state dependant memories, or memories that change when the environment around the person changes. The brain remembers tons of things and is an amazing tool for memories.

analysis.pattern_summary: Greyson misses every multiple-choice item on sentence-level logic: choosing the irrelevant sentence (G8.1 Q9) and choosing the right subordinating or coordinating conjunction (G8.4 Q5, G8.5 Q6, G8.6 Q5, where "and" was chosen over a subordinator). The same surface-level errors recur: misspellings (Kenye, collage, wich, sping, tadition, dicoverd, doug), homophone and usage errors (their/there), missing capitalization and apostrophes (i've, christmas, Yacoubas), and run-on or tangled syntax ("which I thought was really it was very cool," "dayso"). Sentences are also underdeveloped. Graders repeatedly suggest adding a reason, detail, or example, and Hayden's combined sentences (Q5 in G4.1) are comma-spliced or awkward. Paragraph responses are organized but contain editing errors that keep the score just under the threshold.
analysis.skill_gaps: spelling of grade-level and high-frequency words, homophones (their/there), capitalization of proper nouns and holidays, possessive apostrophes, run-on and comma-splice correction, sentence combining with because/but/so, elaboration (adding a reason or detail), revising for clarity and sentence fluency, proofreading and editing, fragment expansion, answering the prompt directly (e.g., the "No, I do not have…" response), appositive punctuation

The disconnect is that the quizzes likely test isolated skills with 1–2 attempts and no scores recorded (best/latest = None), while the tests require applying those skills in open writing along with spelling and proofreading, which the plan does not target.

- Commonly Confused Words and Homophones (Language G4): targets their/there and similar usage errors.
- Possessive Nouns and Proper Noun Capitalization (Conventions G4): addresses Yacoubas/Yacouba's, i've, and christmas.
- Elaborating Sentences with Reasons and Details (Sentences G4 / Writing Brainlift): addresses repeated feedback to add a reason or example, using because/so and appositive combinations with correct comma punctuation.

analysis.pattern_summary: Hendrix repeatedly misses sentence-level tasks that require following a specific structural instruction. He wrote "so" instead of "since," used "black" set off by commas instead of a true appositive, and picked "became" as the appositive. He also misses mechanics, such as the missing question marks, the "on/no" typo, a comma splice, and an unclear question in Q3 on G3.4. On open-response and paragraph items, his answers are minimal, lack reasons ("because I like the name"), or are blank or "idk," and the three long-response prompts (G3.4 Q11, G3.5 Q11, and similar) went unanswered. Together these show gaps in both skill and stamina or effort, and these gaps keep him stuck at about 27–51%.
analysis.skill_gaps: appositive identification and construction, combining sentences with specified subordinating conjunctions (since), converting statements to interrogatives, end punctuation and proofreading, run-on and comma splice correction, explaining reasoning and text evidence in one-sentence responses, writing complete sentences, paragraph writing from a prompt, writing stamina and persistence on extended responses, spelling
analysis.alphawrite_vs_test: Hendrix shows as MASTERED in Combining Sentences, Identify Appositives, and both Paragraph skills, yet he still misses appositive and conjunction-based combining items and leaves paragraph prompts blank on tests. This suggests the AlphaWrite mastery is not transferring, likely because those quizzes were completed with a single attempt, were possibly rushed, or were easier and more scaffolded than the open-ended test format. (The recorded scores are also None, so the mastery data may be unreliable.)
analysis.rushing_impact: Rushing very likely had a major impact, since the blank or "idk" responses, unproofread errors like "on sign," and ignored directions such as "since" and appositive point to effort and attention problems more than pure skill deficits.
analysis.recommended_activities:
- Identify and Write Appositives (Sentences G3): he picked "became" and used "black" as an appositive, so he needs to relearn and practice identifying and constructing noun-renaming phrases, with redo quizzes that require real scores.
- Combine Sentences Using Subordinating Conjunctions (Combining G3): he swapped "so" for the required "since," so he needs practice following the specified connector (since, because, although, when).
- Statements to Questions and Sentence Types (Sentences G3): he left off question marks and created a confusing hybrid question, so he needs to practice inversion with do/did/should and ending punctuation.
- Proofread and Fix Run-ons and Comma Splices (Sentences G3): he made spelling, punctuation, and comma-splice errors that were easy to catch, so editing practice with a checklist would help.
- Write Paragraph From Prompt with Topic Sentence and Details (Paragraphs G3): he submitted blank paragraph responses, so he needs scaffolded, timed paragraph drafting with an outline, plus the "answer + because + text evidence" frame for one-sentence responses.

analysis.pattern_summary: Hudson's errors are mostly in sentence-level mechanics and precision. He drops or garbles words ("have to something different," "can live Texas," "is Seattle"), makes verb-tense and agreement errors ("Did shawl dances began"), and makes spelling and homophone errors (there/their, no/know, are/our). He also has trouble with targeted sentence-construction tasks (appositives, comma splices, subordinate clause completion, fragment expansion, word order), and his short-response answers often lack the specific reason or text-based explanation the prompt asks for (G4.5 Q6/Q7/Q9, G4.4 Q9, G4.6 Q10). Paragraph responses (Q11) are organized, but they stay generic and don't develop evidence, and they show recurring errors in grammar and spelling.
analysis.skill_gaps: appositive phrase construction, comma splice and run-on correction, complete-sentence revision (missing words/verbs), subordinate clause completion, fragment expansion, verb tense and agreement after auxiliary verbs, word order and sentence clarity, spelling and homophones (their/there, know/no, our/are), capitalization and proofreading, text-based explanation of lessons and reasons, elaboration with specific textual evidence in paragraphs, answering the question's specific demand in short responses
analysis.alphawrite_vs_test: Hudson is marked MASTERED on Combine Sentences in AlphaWrite (only 1 attempt, no recorded score), yet he repeatedly loses points on combining and appositive tasks (G4.3 Q2, G4.4 Q3, G4.5 Q3, G4.6 Q3). That suggests the mastery was shallow, or that the skill isn't transferring to the more specific formats tests use (appositives, comma splices, correct word order) and to carefully proofread output.
analysis.rushing_impact: Rushing probably had a modest effect, since the rushed tests (G4.4 at 81%, G4.6 at 77%) scored in line with his non-rushed ones (76–82%), though they did contain careless errors (lowercase start, misspellings, dropped words) that rushing likely made worse.
analysis.recommended_activities:
- Combine Sentences Using Appositives (Sentences G4/G5): he repeatedly misses appositive construction and defaults to comma splices or incomplete sentences, and his single "mastered" attempt isn't enough evidence.
- Fix Fragments and Run-Ons / Comma Splices (Sentences G4): G4.2 Q2, G4.4 Q2, and G4.5 Q3 show trouble expanding fragments and joining clauses correctly.
- Complete the Sentence with Subordinating Conjunctions (Sentences G4): his completions of "If..." and "Since..." clauses are missing words or are ungrammatical (G4.1 Q4, G4.2 Q3).
- Proofreading and Editing Checklist Practice (Writing Brainlift): targets dropped words, capitalization, spelling, homophones, and verb forms (did + base verb), which cost him points on nearly every test.

analysis.pattern_summary: Iker has stayed in the loop because he does not follow the transformation the prompt asks for. He answers with a statement when asked for a question (G3.2 Q3, G3.4 Q3, G3.5 Q1), and he writes loosely related content instead of doing the operation (G3.4 Q1, Q3, and Q5 turned into paragraphs). He also misses the target structure in combining tasks. He joins ideas with "and" instead of using "since," "because," or an appositive, or he reverses the cause/effect direction (G3.4 Q2, G3.5 Q4, G3.6 Q2 and Q3). Underneath this are recurring sentence-level problems: fragments without a subject or verb ("Nervus happy and popular," "To stay away from predators"), subject-verb and noun agreement, its/it's, and spelling. He also left two items blank on G3.2 and gave "imperative" for a declarative sentence.
analysis.skill_gaps: Rewriting statements as questions (inverting subject and verb), following task directions and staying on the prompt, combining sentences with specified subordinating conjunctions (since/because) and keeping cause and effect in the right direction, writing appositives (renaming noun phrase set off by commas), identifying appositives, identifying sentence types (declarative/interrogative/imperative), writing complete sentences with explicit subjects in short-response answers, subject-verb and noun-number agreement, its/it's and basic spelling/proofreading, giving a reason that explains the "why", task persistence (blank responses)
analysis.alphawrite_vs_test: Iker has "mastered" nearly every relevant G3 AlphaWrite skill (conjunctions, combining sentences, appositives, fragments, unscramble), yet he still scores 50% or lower on the same skills in test items. This suggests the mastery is shallow or isolated (scaffolded, with no scores recorded), and it does not transfer to open-response items that require him to read the prompt carefully, apply the target structure, and proofread. The AlphaWrite data also shows null scores, so mastery cannot be verified.
analysis.rushing_impact: Three of the four tests (G3.4, G3.5, G3.6) were flagged as rushed, and rushing probably contributed substantially to the careless errors (off-prompt paragraphs, missing words, its/it's, spelling, fragments). However, the same structural misses also appeared on the one non-rushed test (G3.2), so rushing is an aggravating factor rather than the sole cause.

Responses to the personal-opinion prompts are either unsupported ("none applies to my life") or overextended, and in G4.2 Q5 he did not complete the "because..." fragment with a text-based reason. analysis.alphawrite_vs_test: Jackson has mastered AlphaWrite skills like paragraph writing from a prompt, changing sentence type, and writing topic sentences from details, yet he still loses points on tests for sentence boundaries, conjunction use, and paragraph structure. The disconnect is that he succeeds on guided, single-skill practice but does not transfer it to independent, timed, text-based writing, where he does not proofread or break up long sentences. analysis.pattern_summary: Jackson stays in the loop because of short written responses. He often gives sentence fragments or answers that don't match the prompt (e.g., "How many bears people can take," "Because every page kids could write thier names," "A beautiful geode, a rock with..."). He also doesn't explain *why* or *what it shows* when asked (G3.4 Q6, Q8, Q10), and he makes sentence-transformation errors (the interrogative rewrite asked about the wrong topic, an incomplete conjunction combine, a general question). His paragraph responses are his strongest area (55% → 85% → 90%), so the problem is control of single-sentence precision and spelling/conventions, not extended writing.
analysis.skill_gaps: complete sentence formation (fragments, subordinate clause "Because..." standing alone), fragment-to-sentence revision (adding a verb), interrogative transformation that preserves the original content, combining sentences with conjunctions, appositive construction, adding reasoning/explanation ("why") to one-sentence answers, directly answering the prompt with a full-sentence stem, spelling and conventions (their, golden, because, it's, beacuse, facinated, Maily), run-on/choppy sentences and punctuation in paragraphs
analysis.alphawrite_vs_test: No AlphaWrite data was provided, so any mastery claim is limited. Test results do show a disconnect: Jackson can write strong, organized paragraphs (85–90%) but still misses basic sentence-level skills (fragments, conjunctions, question transformation) on the same tests, which suggests he may not apply sentence-level skills when writing quickly or in short responses. If AlphaWrite shows sentence-level skills as mastered, the gap is transfer rather than knowledge.
analysis.rushing_impact: Rushing can't be confirmed from the data given, but the unfinished answers (e.g., "The book had golden spines," with a trailing comma) and the many spelling errors suggest that haste or lack of proofreading probably cost him several points on the short-answer items.
analysis.recommended_activities:
- Fragments and Complete Sentences (Sentences G3): fragments like "A beautiful geode, a rock with..." and "Because every page..." show he doesn't reliably identify a missing subject, verb, or independent clause.
- Combine Sentences Using Conjunctions (Sentences G3): the G3.5 Q3 response (0%) stopped before adding "and colorful pages," showing he needs practice combining two ideas into one complete sentence.
- Combine Sentences Using Appositives (Sentences G3/G4): the G3.5 Q4 appositive was attempted correctly but needs refinement, and the sentence didn't preserve the original idea ("still popular").
- Turn Statements into Questions (Sentences G3): both interrogative rewrites (G3.4 Q3, G3.5 Q1) changed or generalized the content instead of reorganizing the original sentence.
- Writing Brainlift: Answer + Because Explanation Sentences (Writing Brainlift): G3.4 Q6, Q8, and Q10 each lost points for not explaining why; practice with a "claim + because/which shows" frame and a proofreading checklist (complete sentence, spelling, punctuation) before submitting.

analysis.pattern_summary: Jacob repeatedly loses points on sentence-level tasks that follow a specific directive: combining sentences with *because/but/so* (0% on G3.1 Q4, G3.2 Q10 and G3.9 Q5), appositives (50% on G3.1, G3.5 and G3.6), and rewriting a statement as a question (0-50% on G3.1, G3.5, G3.6 and G3.9). He often writes a reasonable sentence but ignores the required structure (e.g., "While…" instead of *because*, a comma splice, "Did you know that…" with a period). His short responses stall at about 67% because they lack a developed reason, and his paragraphs have good organization but contain fragments ("Such as…"), informal asides, and some inaccurate or unsupported details. Recurring mechanics errors (subject-verb agreement, lowercase "i", missing end punctuation, spelling) and blank responses (G3.1 Q4, G3.5 Q2) keep him just below mastery on each attempt.
analysis.skill_gaps: appositive phrases, combining sentences with because/but/so (subordination vs. comma splice), converting statements to questions (form and "?"), following the exact task directive, sentence fragments, subject-verb agreement, capitalization and end punctuation, spelling of grade-level words, elaborating a reason or explanation in one-sentence responses, paragraph elaboration and text-evidence accuracy, formal tone in paragraphs, task persistence (blank responses)
analysis.alphawrite_vs_test: No AlphaWrite data was included, so mastery there can't be confirmed. The test data does show a disconnect: Jacob writes organized paragraphs (60-90%) but misses the discrete sentence-combining, appositive and question-formation items that these paragraphs depend on. Any AlphaWrite mastery of those skills is not transferring to timed tests, and a check of his AlphaWrite results on them is needed.
analysis.rushing_impact: Seven of the eight tests were flagged as rushed, and many of his losses were careless (blank answers, missing question marks, "i", "migh", "loking", "becuase"), so rushing likely cost him a meaningful share of points, though not the underlying gaps in appositive and conjunction use.

skills.skill: Identify Topic Sentence And Sequence Details

analysis.pattern_summary: Jagger's paragraph responses are strong (85–95% on the Q11 tasks in G4.1–G4.3), but he repeatedly loses points on sentence-level tasks. He cannot form appositives (0% and 50%, where he gave a prepositional phrase or a comma-separated location instead of a renaming phrase). He also makes subject-verb agreement errors when expanding fragments ("dedication and impact... was," "wildflower... are"), and he makes punctuation and comma errors when combining sentences ("because his efforts, enrollment has doubled"). His short-response items (33%) show weak logic and precision ("so predators could get it," "evolve"), and his G4.4 paragraph lacked text-specific evidence (50%). Taken together, these gaps show a stall on sentence-level grammar and precision, not on general writing ability.
analysis.skill_gaps: appositive phrases, subject-verb agreement (compound and singular subjects), fragment expansion with correct verb agreement, comma use in combined sentences, subordinating conjunction logic (because/so/but), proofreading and spelling (recieved, enourmous, Tachichi, texas), copying text details accurately, precise word choice and logical meaning in short responses, text evidence and specific details in paragraphs
analysis.alphawrite_vs_test: AlphaWrite shows Combine Sentences, Kernel Expansion, Fragment Or Sentence, and Subordinating Conjunctions as mastered, yet he still makes errors on these tasks in timed written tests. The disconnect is that he can recognize or construct these in isolated, scaffolded practice (with no recorded scores, just "MASTERED" after 1 attempt), but he does not transfer them to open-ended production or self-check for agreement and punctuation. Appositives do not appear in the skill plan at all, so that gap is never practiced.
analysis.rushing_impact: Three of the four tests (G4.1, G4.2, G4.4) were rushed, and the careless errors (agreement, spelling, copying "steady" for "ready," capitalization) were likely a substantial cause of the lost points, though the appositive gap would persist even without rushing.
analysis.recommended_activities:
- Appositive Phrases / Combine Sentences Using Appositives (AlphaWrite Sentences G4/G5): he scored 0% and 50% on appositive items, and the skill is not in his mastered plan.
- Subject-Verb Agreement in Complete Sentences (AlphaWrite Sentences G4): he repeatedly mismatches verbs with compound and singular subjects when expanding fragments.
- Kernel Expansion with Self-Edit Checklist (AlphaWrite Sentences G4): re-practice fragment expansion with production and proofreading for agreement, spelling, and capitalization, not just recognition.
- Subordinating Conjunctions: Because/But/So Combining with Comma Rules (AlphaWrite Sentences G4): fixes the misplaced commas and the illogical "so" clause meanings.
- Elaborate Paragraphs with Text Evidence (Writing Brainlift): builds specific details and quotes from the text into paragraphs, addressing the 50% on G4.4.

More soils include Soil with a lot of silt with evaporates after a while.

it evens out the amount of air and water and includes much humus.

For a long period of time, many people have played a game so called Pokémon.

The game originated from Satoshi Tajiri. he yearned of creating a game that was interesting and exciting.

As a child, Tajiri enjoyed insects. He would spend hours trying to catch one. He loved them so much his friends called him "Dr. bug."

He would always say, "Every new bug was a mystery." Collecting bug made him feel rewarded.

When he grew older, he enjoyed playing video games. He learned coding to make his own games. He thought most games were boring and not exciting enough.

He wanted to make something everybody could enjoy. He remembered about his old insect collection and decided to use that as insperation.

He then created a game. In the game, players look for characters called Pokémon. There were over 150 Pokémon to collect.

Players threw Pokéballs at the little creatures and would catch them. Players could also trade with eachother.

The game had a slogan, and that was "Gotta catch 'em all!" For Tajiri, Pokémon were just like collecting bugs. He wished that players would feel the same happiness he felt as a kid.

The game became a very big thing, selling millions of copies. It then turned into a card game, an and app, and then a TV show. It even became a movie!

Tajiri turned a love for bugs, into an amazing game that to this day, is still popular.

In the passage "Dive into a Sunken Museum" by Gail Skroback Hennessey, readers learn about artist Jason deCaires Taylor's unusual underwater sculptures.

questions.student_answer:
An artist named Jason deCaires Taylor has created over 500 life-size statues. But these are not normal statues, they are under the sea!

Jason has created two statue parks under the Caribbean Sea. The first one has 65 statues, it's nearby Grenada. The other one, in Cancun, Mexico, has almost 500 statues. It holds the record for the largest underwater statue park ever.

If you want to see these amazing statues up close, you must bring scuba or snorkel gear. Or if you don't want to get wet, You can also take a glass-bottom boat.

Why make statues under the sea you ask? Jason wants to protect coral reefs. Every single year, many swimmers go under and visit the reefs. But when admiring them, they accidently hurt them without knowing it. So if people swin to the statues instead, the reefs will be safe.

A seven-year-old kid named Sam Clarke decided to visit the park in Grenada. 'I wore a mask and snorkel,' Sam said. 'On my feet I wore fins that helped me swim.'

Sam saw a lot of statues. His favorite was the Circle Of Children. It is twenty-six children including both boys and girls stand in a circle, Holding hands under the ocean.

If you take a look at the statues faces, you can spot that have their eyes closed. That is because the children who posed for the statues had to keep their eyes closed while Jason made the mold. It took two hours.

Not long after, they were put into the ocean. Soon after, ocean life began to take them over and climb onto the statues and cover them. Sponges and seaweed grew on them, and many fish started to visit. After a while, life took over the statues.

And was Jason bothered by the sea life covering his art? 'No,' Jason says. 'I like it most of all. Each visit is new, because the sea changes the art.'

The longer paragraph tasks (Q11) score 70-85%, but the one-sentence prompts score 33-67%. Their answers are often fragments ("Because, it makes children happy," "Listening to what guides tell you"), have no capital letters or end punctuation ("no, because…", "yes, but…", "i would have", "pokemon", "africa"), or give vague reasons ("it was nice," "baby seals are cute"). They also sometimes miss the task directive, as when asked to change the verb "looked" and instead adding adverbial detail. Because every test shows the same mechanics and complete-sentence errors, the loop persists.
analysis.skill_gaps: complete sentences vs. fragments, capitalization (sentence starts, proper nouns, "I"), end punctuation and spacing after periods, restating the question in a full-sentence answer, supporting a claim with a specific reason or example, conjunction use (because/but) in a complete sentence, following the task directive (e.g., strong verb substitution), concise revision (removing redundancy), spelling and homophones (its/it's, trevel, Garissa), pronoun and referent accuracy (him vs. Sally), editing and proofreading

questions.title: Extended text (written response)
questions.prompt:
Passage referenced: "The Library on the Lake" (Stimulus S1).

Write an **expository essay** explaining how the new lakeside library changed life in the city.

Use information from the passage to describe at least three impacts (e.g., learning opportunities, cultural activities, local economy). Organize your ideas clearly and support them with details from the text.

**Make sure your response includes the following**:

**Write 5 clear paragraphs**: Introduction with a strong thesis, 3 body paragr
questions.student_answer:
In the article The Library on the Lake the new lakeside library integrates books, arts, and learning opportunities into a city that would not have had it otherwise. The library, a once forgotten warehouse, became a busy place for community life. The new library changes daily life in the city and proves that a good idea with careful planning can change the story of a place.

Firstly, this library, one that holds many books, serves as a place for citizens to read in silence. Consequently, it helps to educate the city and also provide stories of foriegn culture. According to the text, "Now, they surrounded shelves of books, small reading corners, and wide tables for study."

Furthermore, the library is a place that nurtures art and creative expression. For example, artists often paint along the walls, while musicians would play music in the open atrium. According to the text,"Local artists hung colorful paintings along the walls" and,"Musicians sometimes played in the open atrium."

Above all, the library provides learning opportunities and fun, educational activities or workshops. These workshops were made to nurture creativity for all ages. According to the text," Workshops... taught skills from boatbuilding to computer design.

In conclusion, the new library changes daily life in the city by providing books, arts, and learning opportunities. It changes a small, unnoticed city into a busy and lively travel destination. Citizens will likely continue to support and learn from their new library, because of the major impact that it has made on their daily life.
questions.feedback: Your essay clearly explains that the library improved city life through books, art, and workshops. The introduction gives a focused main idea, and each body paragraph stays centered on one impact. To make your explanation stronger, add a sentence after each piece of evidence that explains exactly how it changes life for residents. For example: “Because people can learn skills such as boatbuilding and computer design, the library helps residents gain useful knowledge and explore new interests.” Your conclusion effectively returns to the idea that the library made the city more active and lively.

questions.prompt:
Write an **expository essay** explaining how people’s food preferences develop and change over time.

Organise your ideas clearly and support them with details from the text.

**Make sure your response includes the following**:

**Write 5 clear paragraphs**: Introduction with a strong thesis, 3 body paragraphs with topic sentences, and a conclusion (5 points)

**Use evidence and explain it**: Support each point with facts or examples from the passage and explain what they show (5 points)

**Stay
questions.student_answer:
In the article Don't Give Up on Broccoli, the author explains how people's food preferences change over time. They explain that with three main reasons: the flavor window, taste-flavor learning, and social learning, which all have their different effects on us. All three contribute to our developing food preferences and are the primary reasons for our changing taste buds.

Firstly, the flavor window, a period from four to six months of age when babies are most open to trying new foods, is when we begin to shape our likes and dislikes about different foods. Although the window gradually closes, it has been proven to reopen later in life, leading to changes in our preferences later on in life. According to the text,"Offering a variety of flavors during this stage helps infants accept unfamiliar tastes later in life."

Secondly, taste-flavor learning is a way of connecting foods we already like to new and unfamiliar ones. This allows for us to combine something we already like with something that we are unceartain about, which helps us learn to like new flavors. According to the text,"Scientists have identified three ways people learn to like flavors... The second is taste-flavor learning,"

Finally, social learning is based on the idea that people tend to enjoy what friends and family enjoy. For example, babies whose mothers drank carrot juice are more likely to enjoy carrot flavored foods, which proves that social learning can teach us to like or dislike new flavors. According to the text,"People tend to enjoy what friends and family enjoy even beginning before birth."

In conclusion, our food preferences are mainly shaped by three parts that each contribute to our ever-growing taste buds. Through the flavor window, taste-flavor learning, and social learning, our food-related likes and dislikes continue to develop from ages one to 100. People all around the world continue to eat and discover new foods because our taste buds never stop growing!
questions.feedback: You clearly explain how the flavor window, taste-flavor learning, and social learning shape food preferences, and your carrot-juice example is especially strong. Your introduction gives a focused main idea, and each body paragraph stays centered on one way tastes develop. To make the essay flow more smoothly, use transitions that show how the ideas connect instead of only “Firstly,” “Secondly,” and “Finally”; for example, write, “As people grow older, taste-flavor learning can continue changing preferences after the flavor window closes.” Your conclusion effectively brings the three ideas together and reinforces that food preferences can keep changing throughout life.

questions.title: Extended text (written response)
questions.prompt:
The question uses the passage "A Day in the Life Aboard the International Space Station" (Stimulus S1).

Based on the passage '*A Day in the Life Aboard the International Space Station*', write an **expository essay** explaining **how astronauts adapt their daily routines to living in microgravity aboard the International Space Station**.

Organise your ideas clearly and support them with details from the text.

**Make sure your response includes the following**:

**Write 5 clear paragraphs**: I
questions.student_answer:
In the article A Day in the Life Aboard the International Space Station, the author explains how astronauts adapt their daily routines to life aboard the ISS. By adapting their basic hygiene, scientific research, and excercise practices, these astronauts work through the challenges of daily life in space. Although life on the ISS is very different from life on Earth, astronauts rely on their adapted routines to stay focused and safe.

To remain clean, astronauts adapt their basic hygiene despite the difficulties of microgravity. They do this by using items like pouches for water to wash their hands or no-rinse soap to clean themselves. According to the text," Water floats in small drops, so astronauts squeeze it into pouches and wipe themselves with no-rinse soap."

Due to the special experiments that microgravity offers, astronauts spend a large part of each day on scientific research. They adapt their research to microgravity by using special wires, tubes, and instruments that are secured to the cabin so that they don't float away. According to the passage," Wires... are secured so they do not drift around the cabin."

Finally, to remain strong and active throughout the day, excercise is essential for astronauts when in space. Engineers adapt excercising equipment by securing them to the floor and walls, allowing astronauts to excercise frequently. According to the article," Astronauts work out... using a treadmill with a harness, a stationary bicycle, and a resistance device."

In conclusion, astronauts use their adapted routines to manage their daily life outside of Earth. By changing the way they clean themselves, study and perform research, and excersise, astronauts stay focused and safe despite their adapted lives. Astronauts prove that adaptability and hard work make it possible to live and work while orbiting far above the planet.
