questions.title: Extended text (written response)
questions.prompt:
The passage *The Road Ahead: How Self-Driving Cars Work* explains how self-driving cars work and discusses their potential benefits and concerns.

Write an expository essay explaining why it is important for readers to understand both the benefits and concerns of self-driving car technology before self-driving cars become more common.

Organise your ideas clearly and support them with details from the text.

**Make sure your response includes the following**:

**Write 5 clear paragraphs**: Intro
questions.student_answer:
Self-driving cars are becoming more common every day, so it is very important for readers to understand both the benefits and concerns of these vehicles as they grow in popularity and use. The article, The Road Ahead: How Self-Driving Cars Work, explains how these cars function, save lives, and also make mistakes. Because of their place as the future of driving, it is essential to understand their helpful impacts, harmful impacts, and the mixed views of these cars held by experts.

Beginning with their helpful impacts, these self-driving cars allow for elderly people who have lost their licenses to travel independently. This can also apply for people with disabilities that would otherwise prevent them from traveling. According to the article,"The technology could also help people who cannot drive.". Experts believe that this could possitively impact many peoples lives.

On the other hand, many critics have serious concerns about these cars, often because of documented failures in their technology. For example, in 2018, a self-driving test vehicle struck and killed a pedestrian in Arizona. According to the text,"The car's sensors detected the person, but the software failed to react in time." which led to difficult questions about safety and trust.

Because of their various impacts, many experts hold different views on self-driving cars. While some believe that they are dangerous because of their mistakes, others believe that they will bring a helpful change to driving. Ultimately, there is no right answer, there are only facts that experts continue to debate about. According to the article,"Some experts believe new jobs will be created in technology and maintenance. Others are not so sure." which highlights the different views.

In conclusion, the benefits and concerns about these new cars are very important for readers to know, as they will become the future of driving. Many people believe that these cars will change dissabled drivers lives for the better, while others view them as major safety hazards. Above all, the future of driving is already here, and understanding both sides is more important than ever.

questions.title: Extended text (written response)
questions.prompt:
Read the passage ***The Robotics Club That Changed a School***.

Write an **expository essay** explaining **how the robotics club changed Lincoln Middle School and its students**.

Use information from the passage to describe at least **three ways the club made a difference**. Organize your ideas clearly and support them with details from the text.

**Make sure your response includes the following**:

**Write 5 clear paragraphs**: Introduction with a strong thesis, 3 body paragraphs with topic s
questions.student_answer:
There have been schools that have introduced a robotics club to their extracarricular activities. The robotics club changed Lincoln middle school in three major ways.

The First way the robotics club changed Lincoln Middle School and its students is by teaching students in the robotics club how to problem solve better. I know this because the author stated in the text "A retired engineer from the neighborhood volunteered to help, teaching them how to troubleshoot problems and think like inventors." This shows how impactful the robotics club was on students ability to problem solve, which may lead to better designs and ability to fix different problems.

The second major way the robotics club changed Lincoln Middle School and its students is by improving the way students are learning. The text stated "Teachers reported that club members asked more questions in science class and showed greater patience when solving problems." This shows that the robotics club impacts other aspects of school, not just robotics and inventing.

The third and final way the robotics club improved Lincoln Middle School and its students is by opening new doors for students and their career paths. The  text showed that "Former members have gone on to study engineering and computer science." This shows that because of the robotics club, members found successful career paths that they may otherwise have not found.

Lincoln Middle School, along with its students, was improved by the robotics club due to the robotics club helping students understand problem solving and inventing, helping them learn more effectively as they were prompted to ask more questions about problem solving, and it opened up new career paths for members of the club. Based on this, more schools should be making the addition of a robotics club to their school.
questions.feedback: You clearly explain three important changes caused by the robotics club: stronger problem-solving, better learning habits, and new career paths. Your quotations from the passage are well chosen, and you explain how each one supports your point. To make the essay flow more smoothly, use more varied transitions instead of relying mostly on “The First,” “The second,” and “The third.” For example, you could begin a paragraph with “Beyond improving problem-solving skills, the club also helped students become more engaged in science class.” Your conclusion effectively brings your three main ideas together and leaves the reader with a final thought about other schools starting robotics clubs.

questions.title: Extended text (written response)
questions.prompt:
Read the passage ***Making Space for Everyone***. (The passage is titled "Passage" in this document.)

Write an **expository essay** explaining **how Michaela Benthaus's journey to space shows that determination and technology can break barriers**.

Use information from the passage to describe at least **three ways her story demonstrates this idea**. Organise your ideas clearly and support them with details from the text.

**Make sure your response includes the following**:

**Write 5 clear para
questions.student_answer:
Going to space is a dream of many people's. Some people have disablities that would prevent them from doing so, but that didn't stop Michaela Benthaus. Michaela Benthaus's journey to space shows that determination and technology can break barriers.

The first way this is shown is by making changes to equipment to allow someone like Benthaus, who is in a wheelchair, to be able to ride in a rocket and make it to space. The text shows that with the help of Blue Origin, a slide for moving between a wheelchair and a seat, a strap to hold her legs in place, and a strong seat to support her would allow her to fly in a rocket ship and actually go into space. Without this change, Benthaus would not be able to do this.

The next way this is done is by programs that allow individuals to learn on the topic of space engineering, despite any disabilities they may have. The text shows that "She kept studying engineering and joined a training program with the European Space Agnecy in 2024." Because of this program, Benthaus was able to defy the setbacks of her disability and become an astronaut.

The third and final way this is done is by the use of an advanced piece of technology, the New Shepard. The text stated "Michaela Benthaus became the first person in a wheelchair to travel to space. The 33-year old German engineer launched from West Texas on Blue Origin's New Shepard rocket." Without this rocket, it is likely that Benthaus would have never been to space, meaning that not only would she not have a record, but she also wouldn't have been able to fulfill her dreams.

Michaela Benthaus's journey to space truly showed how determination and technology can take people to great measures. She made it to space as the first person in a wheelchair to do so with the power of advanced technology, engineering, and time learning and working hard. Benthaus's trip to space might not be the last as her hard work and dedication may have opened up doors for others.

analysis.pattern_summary: Knox stays in the loop mainly because of weak sentence-level control. He has recurring trouble with appositives (G3.1, G3.5, G3.6), where he writes a comma splice or adds an unrelated "just like..." comparison instead of a naming phrase. He also misapplies subordinating conjunctions (because, since, but) so the logic or meaning is reversed, and he makes frequent verb tense and agreement errors (e.g. "she remember," "help it stand out," "lift its quills"). In short responses and paragraphs he gives a claim but rarely a reason or text-based example, and spelling and capitalization slips are persistent. Scores stay in the 73-82% range, but the 50% and 0% scores on the combining and transforming items keep him from advancing.
analysis.skill_gaps: appositive phrase construction, comma splices/run-on correction, subordinating conjunction logic (because/since/but), sentence transformation (statement to question, concise rewriting), verb tense and subject-verb agreement, adding reasons/examples to support claims, staying focused on the prompt (avoiding off-topic "just like..." tangents), proofreading for spelling and capitalization, paragraph development with text evidence
analysis.alphawrite_vs_test: Knox shows Combine Sentences With Appositives and Write Paragraph From Prompt as mastered in AlphaWrite (1 attempt each, no recorded scores), yet he fails appositive items on three separate tests and his paragraphs are thin and error-prone. Mastery was likely reached too easily and does not transfer to independent, timed writing, where he does not apply or self-check the skill.
analysis.rushing_impact: Three of the five tests (G3.1, G3.2, G3.5) were flagged as rushed, and many of the errors there (uncorrected spelling, unfinished fixes, missing proofreading, copying the original sentence unchanged) look careless, so rushing likely contributed moderately to the lost points, though the appositive and conjunction errors persist on non-rushed tests too and reflect true skill gaps.
analysis.recommended_activities:
- Combine Sentences With Appositives, retake with fresh items (Sentences G3): the 1-attempt mastery did not hold, and he keeps writing comma splices or "just like..." additions instead of a naming phrase beside the noun
- Combine Sentences With Conjunctions: because, but, so (Sentences G3): he reverses cause and effect with "because" and avoids "since," so he needs practice matching the conjunction to the relationship
- Fix Run-Ons and Comma Splices (Sentences G3): his repeated comma-joined sentences need targeted correction practice
- Verb Tense and Subject-Verb Agreement Edit Practice (Grammar/Conventions G3): errors like "she remember," "lift," and "help" appear on nearly every test
- Write Paragraph From Prompt with evidence and revision checklist (Paragraphs G3): the mastery did not transfer, so he should practice adding a reason or text detail, staying on topic, and proofreading before submitting

analysis.pattern_summary: Kolton's scores rose from 68% to 71% to 87%, but his lowest scores come on one-sentence extended responses (Q8-Q10 at 33%). In these he gives an anecdote or a vague claim without the explanation or reason the prompt asks for, such as "honesty isn't bad," "move to Africa," and the story about a friend's worm drawings that never says how someone feels. Paragraph responses (Q11) land at 60-75% because they have a clear structure but lack specific text evidence. Across all three tests he also makes recurring conventions errors: "we we're," "firt," "nemisis," "identicall," "companys," and missing closing punctuation. His first-draft sentences are also basic, as in the plain appositive "the teacher."
analysis.skill_gaps: answering the specific prompt (staying on task rather than telling off-topic anecdotes), explaining reasoning ("because" statements), elaboration with descriptive detail (appositives), text evidence integration in paragraphs, inference and theme statements, spelling of grade-level words, contraction and homophone usage (we're/were), end punctuation and parenthesis/comma control, proofreading and revising, sentence-level precision and transitions
analysis.alphawrite_vs_test: Kolton has mastered nearly every AlphaWrite skill, including Kernel Expansion, Subordinating Conjunctions, Write Sentence From Prompt, and Paragraph From Prompt, yet he still loses points on tests. AlphaWrite appears to build sentence construction on guided tasks, but he does not transfer it to independent, text-based responses that require him to stay on prompt, give evidence, and proofread. The mastery data also shows no scores (None%) and only 1-2 attempts per skill, so mastery may reflect completion more than depth.
analysis.rushing_impact: No rushing data was provided, but the careless errors ("we we're," missing periods, an unclosed parenthesis) and the joking or off-topic answers ("move to Africa," "nemisis Melvin Sneedly") suggest low effort or poor proofreading cost him several points, though the content gaps would likely keep him from top scores even without rushing.
analysis.recommended_activities:
- Writing Responses With Reasons, "Because/So" Sentence Explanations (Sentences G5): he gives claims or stories without explaining why, so he needs practice answering the exact question with a reason.

- Paragraph From Prompt with Text Evidence (Paragraph G5): his Q11 paragraphs are well-organized but lack specific article details, so he should practice citing and explaining evidence.
- Revise and Proofread Checklist (Writing Brainlift): the repeated spelling, contraction, and punctuation slips call for a self-edit routine before submitting.
- Theme and Inference Sentence Frames (Writing Brainlift): his "honesty isn't bad" answer shows he needs to state what a story teaches and support it with a reason.

analysis.pattern_summary: Kylen repeatedly loses points on short constructed-response items in three ways. He writes sentence fragments that begin with "Because," and phrases with no subject or verb (G3.2 Q6/Q7, G3.6 Q6, G3.9 Q7-Q9, G3.14, G3.1). He misses the specific skill a prompt asks for: he uses "so" when told to use "because," uses a comma splice or "because" in place of an appositive, and answers about the team when asked about the fans (G3.5 Q4, G3.6 Q2, G3.9 Q1, G3.11 Q2, G3.12 Q2). He also makes recurring mechanical errors: missing commas and end punctuation, uncapitalized names and sentence starts, run-ons, and misspellings. Paragraphs usually score 60-90% (G3.13, G3.14, and G3.1 Q11 scored 0% because they were blank), but his scores on single sentences stay at 33-67%. Late-cycle tests (G3.13, G3.14, G3.1) show a sharp drop, with blank or minimal responses on several items, which suggests disengagement or avoidance. This adds to the skill gaps.
analysis.skill_gaps: appositive construction (set off with commas, renamed noun), complete-sentence restatement of the question (avoiding "Because..." fragments), following the specific conjunction or structure named in the prompt, run-on and comma-splice correction, end punctuation and comma use, capitalization of proper nouns and sentence starts, proofreading and spelling of high-frequency and passage words, explaining the "why" or lesson rather than quoting or listing, staying on the prompt's subject, writing stamina and task persistence (blank responses)
analysis.alphawrite_vs_test: Kylen is marked MASTERED in every AlphaWrite quiz, including basic conjunctions, combining sentences, appositive writing and combining, and sentence-type changes, yet he still fails the same skills on tests. He makes appositive errors on G3.5, G3.9, G3.11 and G3.12, conjunction errors on G3.6, and punctuation errors on G3.4. The skills do not transfer to independent, open-ended writing, and the mastery data show no best or latest scores, so the "mastered" status may be unreliable.
analysis.rushing_impact: Rushing probably had a moderate effect: G3.6, G3.9 and G3.13 were rushed, and G3.13 (36%), with its truncated "Som" and blank responses, was clearly hurt, while the other rushed tests (71-72%) show the same errors as his unrushed tests.
analysis.recommended_activities:
- Combine Sentences Using Appositives (Sentences G3-G5): he keeps writing comma splices or substituting "because" for the appositive, so he needs practice with the noun-renaming, comma-set-off structure under varied prompts.
- Write Complete Sentence Answers / Restating the Question (AlphaWrite Sentences G3): his "Because..." fragments and phrase-only answers cost points on nearly every short-response item.
- Combine Sentences With Basic Conjunctions, specified-word tasks (AlphaWrite Combining G3-G4): he swaps "so" for "because" and omits connectors, so he needs to practice the exact conjunction given in the prompt.
- Fix Run-ons and Comma Splices / Punctuating Compound Sentences (AlphaWrite Editing G3-G4): he repeatedly omits commas before "so" and "then" and joins sentences with commas alone.
- Writing Brainlift: Proofread and Revise Checklist (Writing Brainlift): a short routine for checking capitalization, end marks, spelling and answering exactly what the question asks, which should help with both rushed and unrushed tests.

mastered_in_alphawrite_not_tests.skill: Identify Topic Sentence And Sequence Details

analysis.pattern_summary: Lathan's weakest area is following the specific directive in short-response prompts. He repeatedly misses appositives (G3.3 Q3, G3.5 Q4 and Q5, G3.6 Q3, G3.7 Q4) and swaps in an adverb, "because," "and," or a stray comma instead. He also misses the required connector (G3.7 Q5) and the target verb change (G3.4 Q1). His one-sentence explanations name an event but leave out the "why" or a complete sentence (G3.3 Q7, G3.4 Q8 and Q9, G3.7 Q6 and Q8). Paragraph tasks score well (75-85%) but carry recurring mechanics errors (its/it's, apostrophes, capitalization, comma misuse) and formulaic text-evidence use.
analysis.skill_gaps: appositive construction and identification, following the exact prompt directive (task compliance), sentence combining with a specified conjunction (because/but/so), strong or precise verb substitution, explaining "why" in a single complete sentence, complete sentences versus fragments (e.g., starting with "Because"), possessives and apostrophes (its/it's, porcupine's), capitalization and proofreading, comma usage, cause-and-effect reasoning (G3.7 Q6)
analysis.alphawrite_vs_test: Lathan is marked MASTERED on the Appositives (Write and Combine) and Basic Conjunctions quizzes, yet he still scores 0-50% on appositive and conjunction items on tests. This suggests the skill does not transfer from structured quiz formats to open-response prompts, or that he does not read the directive on tests. Mastery was likely reached through recognition or scaffolded support, not independent production. The AlphaWrite data also shows no scores (best/latest = None%), so the mastery flags can't be verified.
analysis.rushing_impact: Four of the five tests (G3.4-G3.7) were rushed, and the many careless errors (a stray comma, skipped directives, "Became" as the appositive, uncapitalized "i", "Thats") suggest rushing substantially lowered scores, though the repeated appositive misses point to a real skill gap as well.
analysis.recommended_activities:
- Combine Sentences With Appositives (Production G3): re-run it with a no-scaffold, timed-check approach, since he is marked mastered but still replaces the appositive with "and" or "because" on tests.
- Write Appositives (Production G3): practice identifying and writing appositives, including the "identify the appositive" format he scored 0% on (G3.5 Q5).
- Basic Conjunctions (Sentences G3): drill choosing the specific conjunction the prompt requires (because/but/so), targeting his G3.7 Q5 miss.
- Writing SPOs (Paragraphs G3): practice the "Say/Prove/Outcome" or sentence-level explanation structure so one-sentence answers include the "why" (G3.3 Q7, G3.4 Q8, G3.7 Q8).
- Proofreading and Conventions Mini-Lessons (Writing Brainlift): focus on its/it's, possessive apostrophes, capital "I," and comma errors, with a "reread the prompt and your answer before submitting" checklist to curb rushed mistakes.

analysis.pattern_summary: Mara's scores rose from 31% to 49% to 78% to 73% across G3.1–G3.4, so the early failures were severe and the later results are borderline. The same gaps recur in every test. Her one-sentence answers state a position but rarely add the "because" reason the graders ask for (G3.2 Q5, Q8; G3.4 Q6, Q8). She also makes frequent conventions and sentence-control errors: missing capitals and end punctuation, misspellings, dropped or extra function words ("popular with in the fans," "forward the Teddy Bear Toss"), and unclear syntax ("making them wont to win"). Her 55–65% paragraph responses (G3.3 Q11, G3.4 Q11) are short, loosely organized, and use few details from the article. She also misses targeted skills like appositives, combining sentences with because/but/so, and concise rewriting, and she misidentified a sentence type (declarative vs. imperative).
analysis.skill_gaps: appositive phrases, combining sentences with because/but/so, concise sentence revision, adding reasons or justification inside one sentence, text-evidence integration in paragraphs, paragraph development and organization (topic sentence, details, conclusion), capitalization and end punctuation, spelling of grade-level words, preposition and function-word accuracy, sentence clarity and completeness, sentence-type identification, stronger verb choice
analysis.alphawrite_vs_test: Every G3 AlphaWrite skill is marked MASTERED after only 1–2 attempts, yet Mara still misses the same skills on tests: combining sentences, elaborating paragraphs, and writing topic sentences. The skills are not transferring to independent writing, so the quizzes may be too scaffolded or too easy to show real mastery. Score data is also missing (best/latest = None), so the mastery labels can't be checked, and the plan is all G3 even though her HMG is G2.
analysis.rushing_impact: No timing or rushing data was provided, so the impact can't be determined, though the many careless errors (capitalization, spelling, dropped words) suggest limited proofreading.
analysis.recommended_activities:
- Combining Sentences with Because/But/So (Combining G3 Basic Conjunctions): she missed this on G3.1 Q4 despite "mastery," so redo it with free-response items and a no-hints condition.
- Appositive Combining Practice (Combining/Sentences G3): she missed the appositive on G3.1 Q1 and wrote a compound sentence instead.
- Elaborate Paragraphs and Write Paragraph From Prompt with article-based evidence (Paragraphs G3): her paragraphs lack text details and organization, so require two or three cited details plus a closing sentence.
- Kernel Expansion with Reasons ("because" expansions) (Sentences G3): she gives opinions without reasons, so practice expanding a short answer into one sentence

skills.skill: Identify Topic Sentence And Sequence Details

mastered_in_alphawrite_not_tests.skill: Identify Topic Sentence And Sequence Details

analysis.pattern_summary: On G3.1, Q1-Q6 were single-letter responses ("as", "z", "g", "h", "j"), so appositive combining, question transformation, sentence revision, and conjunction-based combining were never attempted. When the student did write real sentences (Q7, Q9, and all of G3.2), they capped at about 67-70% because of run-ons and over-long sentences that ignore "write one sentence," faulty parallelism ("going… and play"), and unclear syntax ("change where the people instead of throwing them…"). Conventions errors (exitement, arent, acces, wroten, missing apostrophes, missing commas) and a sentence-type error (calling a declarative sentence "imperative") also hold scores down. Only two attempts are visible in this data, so the loop looks driven mostly by disengagement on G3.1 plus unresolved sentence-level control and conventions.
analysis.skill_gaps: appositive phrases, combining sentences with because/but/so, transforming statements into questions, revising fragments into complete sentences, concise single-sentence responses (run-on control), parallel verb structure, sentence-type identification (declarative vs. imperative), spelling and apostrophe conventions, end punctuation and comma use, paragraph concision and organization
analysis.alphawrite_vs_test: All four Paragraphs G3 skills (topic sentences, transitions, brainstorming) are marked mastered, yet the tests fail on sentence-level skills (combining, revising, conventions, sentence types) that those skills do not cover. The mastered skills also show no recorded scores (best/latest = None%) and only 1-2 attempts, so the "mastered" status is weak evidence of real proficiency.
analysis.rushing_impact: Rushing very likely caused most of the G3.1 failure: six of nine questions got 0% from one-letter answers, while the two real attempts earned 67%, so the score would probably have been around 50-60% with genuine effort.
analysis.recommended_activities: - Combine Sentences Using Appositives (Sentences G3): the student left the appositive question blank and has no evidence of appositive construction.

questions.prompt:
Write an **expository essay** explaining how people are helping monarch butterflies survive.

Use information from the passage to support your ideas.

**Make sure your response includes the following**:

**Write 5 clear paragraphs**: Introduction with a strong thesis, 3 body paragraphs with topic sentences, and a conclusion (5 points)

**Use evidence and explain it**: Support each point with facts or examples from the passage and explain what they show (5 points)

**Stay organized and on topic**
questions.student_answer:
People help monarch butterflies stay alive by building way stations, donating money, and taging butterflies.

The first way that people can help monarch butterflies stay alive are way stations.Way stations are a small garden where monarchs could rest and lay eggs. It's a perfect place for butterflies to rest for birth. It's very important to have way stations so that butterflies can birth healthy eggs.

The next way that people can support monarch butterflies is donating money to monarch butterfly stations. This donated money is used for building way stations, and places to help butterflies rest and stay healthy. These donations are super important so that the butterfly population doesn't get extinct.

The last way people can help monarchs stay alive is by tagging butterflies. People tag butterflies with small stickers, count caterpillars, and record monarch sighting. This can help people see how the monarch butterfly population is doing and how people can help support them more. In conclusion, building way stations, donating money, and tagging can really impact the monarch population in a great way.
questions.feedback: You built a clear, focused essay with a strong thesis that previewed your three ways people help monarchs — way stations, donations, and tagging — and you followed through on each one. Your transitions ('The first way,' 'The next way,' 'The last way,' 'In conclusion') made the essay easy to follow, and you explained why each action matters rather than just listing facts. To grow further, give your conclusion its own paragraph instead of tucking it onto the end of the tagging paragraph, so the essay ends with a clear final beat. Also watch a couple of small slips: 'The first way ... are way stations' should be 'is a way station,' and 'taging' should be spelled 'tagging.' Finally, try swapping casual phrases like 'super important' for more formal wording such as 'essential' or 'critical' to strengthen your academic tone.

analysis.pattern_summary: McKayla scores 0% on nearly every multiple-choice item across six attempts, while her essays land at 55-80%. Her misses cluster in three areas: sentence expansion from a kernel (G6.1 Q5, G6.3 Q5, G6.5 Q10), conjunction and "because" usage (G6.2 Q3, G6.3 Q3, G6.4 Q3, G6.6 Q3), and choosing transitions by logical relationship (G6.2 Q8, G6.3 Q9, G6.4 Q9). She repeatedly picks comma-before-"because" options and contrast or sequence transitions where cause or addition is needed. In the essays, her organization and transitions are solid, but the grader feedback points to thin elaboration, so her writing is formulaic and the sentence-level logic isn't secure.
analysis.skill_gaps: Subordinating conjunction punctuation (no comma before "because"), logical transition selection (cause/effect, contrast, addition), sentence expansion with specific detail rather than generic detail, elaboration and explaining "why" in body paragraphs, relevance and unity (identifying sentences that don't belong), conjunction choice when combining sentences, proofreading for mechanics (spelling such as "taging", agreement, run-ons)
analysis.alphawrite_vs_test: She has mastered Finishing Transition Words and Topic Brainstorm in AlphaWrite, yet she keeps missing transition-selection MCQs (G6.2 Q8, G6.3 Q9, G6.4 Q9) even though she uses transitions well in essays. This suggests the mastery is shallow, with only one attempt and no score recorded, and that she uses memorized ordering transitions ("The first way," "In conclusion") without reasoning about the logical relationship between ideas.
analysis.rushing_impact: Every test was flagged as rushed, and the pattern of 0% on quick-decision MCQs, including repeat misses on "because" items she likely knows, suggests rushing contributed substantially, though the consistency of the errors points to real conceptual gaps beyond carelessness.
analysis.recommended_activities:
- Combine Sentences Using Conjunctions and "Because" (Sentences G5/G6): she misses "because" punctuation and logical-conjunction items on four of the six tests.
- Transition Words: Choosing by Relationship (AlphaWrite): targets cause/effect, contrast, and addition, and replaces her one-attempt mastery with checked practice.
- Expand the Kernel Sentence (AlphaWrite Sentences): she keeps choosing bare or generic expansions over ones with specific, meaningful detail.
- Elaboration and Paragraph Development (AlphaWrite Paragraphs): grader feedback repeatedly asks her to explain "why" and deepen evidence.
- Sentence Relevance and Unity / Delete the Off-Topic Sentence (Writing Brainlift): addresses the G6.5 "does NOT belong" miss and the need to stay focused in paragraphs.

That is a consistent 0% on the highest-weighted item, and it caps his scores regardless of how he does elsewhere. On shorter items he can write complete, relevant sentences but gets only partial credit: he doesn't swap in a stronger verb (Q1), restates the text instead of explaining it (Q6, Q8), and builds the appositive with a "with…" phrase instead of a renaming noun phrase (Q4). He also left the sentence-type transformation (interrogative, Q3) blank and made spelling errors ("excitment").
analysis.skill_gaps: Sustained paragraph writing from a passage prompt (task initiation/persistence), appositive construction (renaming noun phrases), sentence type transformation (declarative to interrogative), precise or vivid verb choice, explaining text evidence in his own words (inference about character), explaining why a moment matters (elaboration), spelling and proofreading, and stamina or effort on long-response items.
analysis.alphawrite_vs_test: Musa has "mastered" all 15 AlphaWrite skills, including paragraph-from-prompt, appositives, change sentence type, and elaboration, yet he still submits blank paragraphs and misses the same skills on tests. The disconnect is likely transfer and effort: he can complete scaffolded, low-stakes tasks but doesn't apply the skills independently to passage-based prompts. The mastery data also shows no scores (best/latest = None), so it may be inflated by few attempts (1–3 each) or by completion-based credit.

analysis.pattern_summary: Nathaniel's scores rose from 67% to 83% and 80%, but he keeps missing the mastery cutoff because of the same weaknesses in extended writing. In every essay, the grader asks for deeper explanation of the quotes he uses (the "WHY"), and his text evidence is dropped in without analysis. His essays also carry many unproofread spelling errors ("Wilkma," "monther," "wining," "animted," "perventing habait," "trackeing," "expamples") and sentence-level slips, such as the awkward, non-parallel thesis with a "you" shift on G6.3. In G6.3 he also missed two multiple-choice items on skills AlphaWrite lists as mastered: a comma before "because" (Q3) and vague elaboration like "doing things" (Q8).
analysis.skill_gaps: explaining/analyzing text evidence (quote → commentary), elaboration with specific detail, paragraph structure and topic sentences, parallel structure in thesis statements, comma use with subordinating conjunctions ("because"), spelling and proofreading, consistent academic voice (avoiding "you"), essay organization and development
analysis.alphawrite_vs_test: All eight AlphaWrite skills (conjunctions, elaboration, combining, outline-to-draft) are marked mastered, yet he still misuses "because" and chooses weak elaboration on the test, so the skills are not transferring to independent writing or to test items. The AlphaWrite data also shows no scores (best/latest = None), so "mastered" may reflect completion rather than demonstrated fluency.
analysis.rushing_impact: Rushing probably had a moderate effect: the G6.1 and G6.3 tests were rushed, and the missed "because" and elaboration items and the many spelling errors are the kind of careless mistakes he likely would have caught with more time, though the persistent lack of evidence explanation points to a genuine skill gap as well.

skills.skill: Production G3 Combine Sentences With Appositives Quiz

analysis.pattern_summary: Nicholas keeps stalling on sentence-level construction. He writes fragments and comma splices, as in "Because the bears scored a goal. Fans tossed…" and "…dogs, their names are…". He also struggles with sentence combining (appositives, conjunctions, and questions), and he often misreads task directives. On identification and recognition items he rewrites the sentence instead of naming the sentence type or the appositive (G3.2 Q4, G3.5 Q5). His paragraph responses are often strong (75–85% on several), but scores drop sharply when he rushes. Rushed attempts produced the 47% on G3.2 and the weaker G3.6 paragraph, which has run-on, comma-joined sentences.
analysis.skill_gaps: appositive construction and identification, combining sentences with conjunctions (fragment avoidance), comma splices and run-on sentences, sentence fragments with subordinating conjunctions ("Because…"), converting statements to questions (inverted word order), reading and following prompt directives (identify vs. rewrite), capitalization of "I", complete-sentence responses to short-answer prompts, factual accuracy and text-based details (e.g., porcupine quills), paragraph sentence variety and cohesion
analysis.alphawrite_vs_test: Nicholas is marked MASTERED on Combine Sentences, Combine With Appositives, Write Appositives, and Freeform Paragraph, yet he still fails appositive and conjunction combining items on tests (G3.5 Q3–Q5, G3.2 Q2/Q10). This suggests the mastery doesn't transfer to unscaffolded, timed contexts, or that the quizzes were passed with limited attempts (1 each, no scores recorded) and without durable retention. The quizzes also appear not to cover identifying skills or fragment and comma-splice control.
analysis.rushing_impact: Rushing likely had a major effect on the lowest-scoring tests, especially G3.2 (47%), where errors like ignoring directives, leaving incomplete answers, and writing fragments are careless slips; the rushed G3.1 and G3.6 attempts also show avoidable mechanical errors.
analysis.recommended_activities:
- Combine Sentences Using Conjunctions (Sentences G3): targets fragments like "Because the bears scored a goal." and comma splices, with practice keeping both clauses in one sentence.
- Write Appositives / Identify Appositives (Sentences G3): reinforces recognizing the appositive (the extra-information phrase) versus rewriting the whole sentence, as missed in G3.5 Q5.
- Combine Sentences With Appositives, Retake with Mixed Review (Sentences G3): the earlier mastery didn't transfer, so use spaced, unscaffolded practice to build retention.
- Fix Run-ons and Fragments / Comma Splices (Sentences G3): addresses recurring run-on and comma-joined sentences in paragraphs (G3.1, G3.6) and short answers.
- Turn Statements into Questions and Answer Question Types (Sentences G3): practice with inverted word order, plus a Writing Brainlift routine of underlining the task verb (identify, rewrite, combine) and checking the response against it before submitting.

analysis.pattern_summary: Oliver is stuck at 76–80% on G3 writing tests because of recurring gaps in sentence-level mechanics and in following the task's exact directive. He rewrites instead of classifying (G3.2 Q4), restates instead of transforming into a question (G3.2 Q3), and gives incomplete or unjustified single-sentence responses (G3.3 Q7, G3.4 Q8 fragment, G3.4 Q6). He also misapplies the subordinating conjunction "since" (comma placement and clause order), does not strengthen verbs (G3.4 Q1), and makes persistent spelling and usage errors ("where" for "were", "workors", "minuts", "would'nt"). His paragraphs hold up better (65–80%) but lack text-specific details.
analysis.skill_gaps: Following prompt directives (task-verb comprehension), converting statements to interrogative sentences, identifying sentence types, subordinating conjunction placement and punctuation ("since"), strong/precise verb choice, writing complete sentences with a stated reason (because-clauses), supporting claims with text evidence and specific details, spelling and usage conventions (were/where, contractions, capitalization), proofreading
analysis.alphawrite_vs_test: Oliver has mastered every G3 skill in AlphaWrite, including Subordinating Conjunctions, Combine Sentences, Fragment or Sentence, and Write Sentence From Prompt, yet he still misses these on tests (e.g., "since" combining, incomplete fragment-like answers). This suggests that mastery in the lesson context (likely scaffolded, with only 1 attempt and no recorded scores) does not transfer to independent, open-response test conditions, and that AlphaWrite may not cover question transformation, sentence-type identification, or conventions.
analysis.rushing_impact: Only G3.3 was flagged as rushed, and it scored 78%, in line with the other tests (76% and 80%), so rushing likely had a minor effect. It may explain the missing "because" reasoning and some careless errors, but it isn't the main cause of the loop.
analysis.recommended_activities:
- Subordinating Conjunctions (Sentences G3): redo with a focus on fronting a "since/because" clause and placing the comma after the clause, not after the conjunction. He misplaced "since," in G3.4 Q2.
- Write Sentence From Prompt (Sentences G3): practice answering exactly what is asked, including sentence-type identification, statement-to-question conversion, and one-sentence answers with a reason, to address G3.2 Q3/Q4 and G3.3/G3.4 one-sentence items.
- Elaborate Paragraphs (Paragraphs G3): practice adding specific article details and evidence to the claims he makes, since his paragraphs are opinion-heavy (Camel Library) or lack detail.
- Fragment Or Sentence (Sentences G3): retry using sentences with a stated "why," to fix fragments like "Laya showing the geode to the guide" (G3.4 Q8).
- Writing Brainlift proofreading/conventions activity (Writing Brainlift): a targeted editing routine for were/where, contractions, and spelling, to address recurring errors that cost points in every test's paragraph.

analysis.pattern_summary: Phoenix Knight scores 71–82% on the G3 tests, but the lost points come from the same gaps each time. First, answers are incomplete: single-sentence responses state a position or choice ("I think the most meaningful moment was...", "nice and curious girl", "leaving cool souvenirs") without the "why" or reason the prompt asks for. Second, the student gives text evidence but does not explain it, as in the "breeze and birds" quote and the bug-collecting detail in the Pokémon paragraph. Third, the student misses direct skill-application items, scoring 0–50% on sentence-type identification (Imperative vs. declarative), appositive rewriting, adding a subordinating conjunction ("Because"), and strengthening a verb. Conventions such as capitalization, possessive/plural apostrophes ("seal's"), spelling, and subject-verb agreement keep costing points on otherwise adequate responses. The 0% items drag down scores on tests that are otherwise near the pass line.
analysis.skill_gaps: Answering all parts of a prompt (claim plus reason), explaining and elaborating on text evidence, appositive phrase construction, subordinating conjunctions and complex sentence completion, sentence type identification (declarative vs. imperative), precise or strong verb choice, plural vs. possessive apostrophes, capitalization and proofreading, spelling, subject-verb agreement, paragraph development beyond restating the prompt
analysis.alphawrite_vs_test: Every AlphaWrite skill (appositives, conjunctions, change sentence type, elaborating paragraphs, text-evidence-style paragraph writing) is marked MASTERED, often after only 1–2 attempts, yet the same skills fail on tests: the appositive rewrite got 50%, the conjunction item 0%, and sentence type 0%. This suggests the student passes the quizzes without retaining the skills or transferring them to unscaffolded, mixed-format test items, and the quizzes may be too easy or allow shallow mastery.
analysis.rushing_impact: No rushing data is provided, but the careless errors (missing capitals, typos, misread directions such as rewriting the full sentence instead of supplying the missing word, and "Imperative" for a plain statement) suggest that rushing or poor proofreading likely cost a modest amount, perhaps a few percentage points, rather than being the main cause.
analysis.recommended_activities:
- Write Appositives / Combine Sentences With Appositives, revisited with a higher bar (Production G3 / Sentences G3-G4): the appositive rewrite scored 50% despite "mastery," so the student needs delayed, mixed-format retesting rather than the same quiz.
- Combining with Subordinating Conjunctions (Combining G3-G4): the "Because/Although" completion scored 0%, and basic-conjunction mastery did not transfer to sentence-opening subordinators.
- Change Sentence Type: identify and label declarative, imperative, interrogative, and exclamatory sentences (Transformation G3): the sentence-type item scored 0% and the student confused a statement with a command.
- Elaborate Paragraphs with "because/this shows" reasoning (Paragraphs G3-G4): the student should practice adding the explanation after each quote or detail and answering both parts of "what and why" prompts in one sentence.
- Proofreading / Editing Checklist for conventions (Writing Brainlift or Conventions G3): targets capitalization, apostrophes (plural vs. possessive), spelling, and subject-verb agreement, with a required self-check before submitting.

analysis.pattern_summary: Quentin's written responses give a correct core idea but stay thin. He rarely adds the "because" reasoning or text evidence that graders ask for (Q6, Q9, Q10 on G3.4), and he does not build a full paragraph with an opening, details, and closing (Q11 on both tests: 50%, then 20%). Mechanics also hold him back: missing capitals, run-together words ("thenbook"), and misspellings ("listining," "competetivenes," "sculports"). The G3.5 appositive item (Q4, 50%) is a further sign that his sentence-level control is inconsistent.
analysis.skill_gaps: elaboration with reasons ("because" statements), text evidence integration, paragraph development (topic sentence, supporting details, concluding sentence), responding fully to extended-response prompts, capitalization and sentence boundaries, spelling and word spacing/proofreading, appositive punctuation and construction, character-trait inference with supporting actions
analysis.alphawrite_vs_test: Quentin shows every G3 Paragraphs and Sentences skill as MASTERED, including Write Paragraph From Prompt and Combine Sentences With Appositives, with only 1 attempt on nearly all of them and no recorded scores. Yet he still writes underdeveloped one-sentence answers and scores 20% on a paragraph prompt, so the skills are not transferring to timed, text-based writing. The "mastered" status may reflect completion rather than real proficiency, and he has not practiced pulling evidence from a passage.
analysis.rushing_impact: The G3.4 test was flagged as rushed, and the missing reasons, unchecked spelling, and abandoned paragraph on Q11 are consistent with that. Rushing probably cost him several points, though the same gaps persist on the unrushed G3.5 (60%), so it is a contributing factor rather than the root cause.
analysis.recommended_activities:
- Write Paragraph From Prompt (Paragraphs G3): redo with a required topic sentence, 2-3 text-based details, and a closing sentence, since Q11 fell from 50% to 20%. Require a re-attempt until the score is recorded, not just completed.
- Write Freeform Paragraph (Paragraphs G3): build stamina and structure in extended responses without scaffolds, with a self-check for capitals, spelling, and spacing before submitting.
- Write Cs From Details (Paragraphs G3): practice concluding sentences and tying details back to the main idea, so his answers don't stop after one sentence.
- Combine Sentences With Appositives (Sentences G3): redo with scored attempts, to solidify comma placement and appositive construction (G3.5 Q4).
- Writing Brainlift sentence expansion with "because" (Evidence and Elaboration): practice adding a reason and a passage detail to a correct claim, as in the Q6, Q9, and Q10 feedback. Add a proofreading checklist (capital letters, spelling, word spacing) to every response.

Production G3 Combine Sentences With Appositives Quiz

analysis.pattern_summary: Rafaela's scores sit in the 80s on every attempt, so the loop comes from short-response items that score 0-67% and keep her below the passing line. Her ideas and content are usually sound, but she repeatedly joins two independent clauses with only a comma (comma splices, run-ons) and cannot reliably produce or identify appositives (G3.3 Q3, G3.5 Q4 and Q5, G3.6 Q3). She also leaves answers incomplete, such as explaining "what" without "why" (G3.4 Q10), and she makes frequent conventions errors: lowercase "i," misspellings, comma after "so," missing apostrophes, and a sentence fragment in G3.3 Q5.
analysis.skill_gaps: appositive identification and construction, comma splices and run-on sentences, sentence combining with coordinating conjunctions (punctuation of "so" and "and"), complete-sentence construction (fragments and missing verbs), single-sentence responses that include a reason or explanation, capitalization and spelling conventions (I, proper nouns, apostrophes), proofreading and revision of her own writing, sentence concision and avoiding repetition
analysis.alphawrite_vs_test: Every AlphaWrite skill is marked mastered, including appositives, conjunction combining, and paragraph writing, yet she still misses appositive and combining items on tests. The disconnect is that she handles scaffolded or isolated practice but does not transfer it to independent, timed, text-based writing, and she does not apply conventions when composing freely.
analysis.rushing_impact: Five of six tests were flagged as rushed, and rushing likely contributed substantially, because many of her errors (lowercase "i," misspellings, comma splices, an incomplete answer) are careless slips she can fix when she slows down.
analysis.recommended_activities:
- Combine Sentences With Appositives (Production G3): she still misses appositive combining on tests (G3.5 Q4, G3.6 Q3) despite earlier mastery, so spaced re-practice with a stricter mastery threshold would help.
- Write Appositives / Identify Appositives (Production G3): she named the verb "became" as the appositive, which shows she cannot identify the noun-renaming phrase.
- Fix Run-Ons and Comma Splices (Sentences G3/G4): she regularly joins complete ideas with only a comma (G3.2 Q9, G3.6 Q7, G3.7 Q1, Q2, Q3), so she needs practice with periods or "and/but/so" after the comma.
- Basic Conjunctions Combining (Combining G3): she needs punctuation practice with "so" and "and" (no comma after "so" in G3.2 Q10; comma plus "and" in G3.7 Q2).
- Revise and Proofread Own Writing (Writing Brainlift): a required checklist before submitting (capital "I," spelling, ending punctuation, one sentence versus two, reason included) would address the rushed, careless errors.

analysis.pattern_summary: Renee's main sentence-level gap is appositives. She misses them on nearly every test (G3.1 Q1, G3.5 Q4 and Q5, G3.6 Q3, G3.7 Q4, G3.8 Q1), usually substituting "and/but/because" or adding a trailing detail instead of a comma-set noun phrase, and in G3.5 she labeled the verb "became" as the appositive. She also repeatedly fails to do the exact transformation asked for (asking a question, using a stronger verb, identifying the sentence type), and her one-sentence responses are often run-ons or omit the required reason (G3.1 Q8, Q10, G3.8 Q9, G3.7 Q9). Her paragraph responses score well (75–90%), so the loop comes from short-response precision, not extended writing. The G3.6 score of 0% looks like a scoring anomaly, since several answers (Q1, Q5, Q6, Q7) appear correct, so that result should be verified before it is counted as a real failure.

analysis.alphawrite_vs_test: AlphaWrite shows every skill as mastered (Change Sentence Type, Combining, Elaborate Paragraphs, Write Paragraph From Prompt, and others), yet he still fails to change a sentence into a correct question, to combine with an appositive, or to elaborate and build a multi-sentence paragraph on tests. The mastery doesn't transfer to independent, text-based writing. The AlphaWrite scores are also all listed as None%, so mastery may reflect completion rather than demonstrated proficiency, and attempt counts are mostly just 1.
analysis.rushing_impact: Two of the three tests (G3.1 and G3.6) were flagged as rushed, and rushing likely contributed to the thin, unelaborated responses and the avoidable grammar and spelling errors. It probably isn't the whole cause, since the unrushed G3.5 test had the same one-sentence response to the paragraph prompt (40%).
analysis.recommended_activities:
- Elaborate Paragraphs (Paragraphs G3): redo with a strict criterion (a topic sentence plus at least 2–3 supporting details) to address the one-sentence paragraph responses on the Q11 tasks, since the earlier mastery didn't carry over.
- Write Paragraph From Prompt (Paragraphs G3): practice answering a text-based prompt in multiple sentences, using details from a passage, to fix the missing text evidence and incomplete responses.
- Combine Sentences Using Appositives (Sentences G4): he substituted "and" for an appositive on G3.5 Q4, so he needs direct instruction and practice with appositive phrases.
- Change Sentence Type (Sentences G3): repeat with a focus on question word order (e.g., "Why can't we…?"), because he mastered this in AlphaWrite but still produced "why we can't".

analysis.pattern_summary: Robert's scores on G4.1 (89%) and G4.2 (88%) were high, so the loop is not caused by a broad writing deficit. It comes from recurring errors in sentence-level revision tasks that stay at 50% or below: turning fragments into sentences while keeping the meaning, adding appositives (he added a purpose phrase, "to see the pretty state flower," or a clause, "but you have to be good at it"), and combining sentences with because/but/so (he used "but" for ideas that don't contrast, and in G4.4 he dropped the conjunction altogether). questions.student_answer: Logos can be popular and common in everyday use. But if we see logos everyday, then why can we not remember them? About 10 years ago, in 2015, 85 students were asked to draw the famous apple logo. Though many of them thought they where right, only 1 of 85 of them could draw it correctly. Lots of the students missed miniscule details, like how many leaves are there and if it has a bite on the apple or not. This wasn't the onlytest that they did. In 1970, many people where requested to draw a perfect picture of the penny. Nearly all the people failed to excecute the perfect penny. But when we see them very often, our brains ignore the small details. This called "attentional saturation". Small details usaually get left out. This is also called gist memory. The gist is the big picture of the logo, not the little details. Overall, logos can be hard to remember, but you can still remember the big picture.

skills.skill: Paragraph From Prompt G4 Write Paragraph From Prompt Quiz

analysis.pattern_summary: Ryann's extended-response answers show good ideas and a clear main point, but conventions and sentence-level control keep costing points. On Q5 (G4.1) she joined two complete ideas with "because of" and a comma splice instead of a conjunction like "so". On Q10 she made another comma splice. On Q4 (G4.2) she left out "to" and misspelled and mis-pluralized words. Across G4.1–G4.3, paragraph responses (Q11) lose points for repeated spelling errors (e.g., "Yaucouba," "becuase," "decited," "suprised," "benifit"). Short-answer responses (Q7, Q8, Q10) score only 67% because she names an idea but doesn't explain it or tie it to herself, for example with "because…".
analysis.skill_gaps: comma splices and run-on sentences, choosing the right conjunction (because/but/so) for cause-effect, combining sentences accurately, spelling and proofreading (including names from the passage), explaining or elaborating ideas ("because" reasoning), appositive construction and grammar (plural agreement, missing "to"), supporting paragraph details with text evidence
analysis.alphawrite_vs_test: Ryann has mastered nearly every relevant AlphaWrite skill (Basic Conjunctions, Combine Sentences, Identify Appositives, Elaborate Paragraphs, Write Paragraph From Prompt), yet she still makes the same errors in her own writing on tests. Her mastery appears to be recognition-level or scaffolded, and it isn't transferring to independent, timed composition and self-editing. The AlphaWrite data also shows no scores (best/latest = None), so "mastered" status may overstate real proficiency.
analysis.rushing_impact: G4.2 was rushed and scored 89%, the highest of the three, with errors like those on the other tests, so rushing probably had minimal impact and the underlying gaps are the main cause.
analysis.recommended_activities:
- Combine Sentences (Sentences G4): Q5 shows she chose the wrong connector and made a comma splice, so she needs practice choosing "so/because/but" for cause-effect and avoiding "because of" between two full clauses.
- Basic Conjunctions (Sentences G4), retake with accuracy focus: it is marked mastered, but the error persists on tests, so repeat it with scores and correction of comma splices.
- Elaborate Paragraphs (AlphaWrite): short responses (Q7, Q8, Q10) lack the explanation or "because" reasoning that graders ask for.
- Write Paragraph From Prompt with a revise/proofread step (AlphaWrite): spelling and name errors in Q11 on all three tests show she needs a self-editing checklist (names, "because," "decided").
- Identify Appositives / Combine Sentences Using Appositives (Sentences G4): Q4 shows she is close but misses grammar details (plural noun, infinitive "to"), so she needs more practice building and checking appositives.

analysis.pattern_summary: Saachi's open-response writing is thin and doesn't follow the task directions. She often skips the specific skill being asked for, for example "so" instead of "since," "and" instead of an appositive, and added details instead of a stronger verb. Her one-sentence answers usually state a claim without a reason ("add why…" feedback on G3.4 Q6, Q8, Q10 and G3.5 Q7). Her paragraphs are short, informal, off-prompt or unsupported, and have no concluding sentence (G3.2 Q11, G3.3 Q11, G3.4 Q11, G3.5 Q11). She also shows sentence-level slips: fragments (G3.2 Q5), a sentence-type error (G3.2 Q4, "exclamatory" for a declarative), and spelling or copying errors (whent, vidio, trucke, thay, fell/feel, spikes/spines). Only G3.4 (49%, rushed) is a clear fail. G3.2 (73%) is a weak pass, and G3.3 (89%) and G3.5 (87%) are near-mastery, so the loop looks driven by persistent misses on 0–50% written-response items rather than broad weakness.
analysis.skill_gaps: appositive production and combining, following the specific skill named in the prompt (subordinating conjunction "since," strong verb substitution), supporting claims with a reason or "because" explanation, paragraph development and concluding sentences, text-evidence integration in article-based paragraphs, complete-sentence writing (avoiding fragments), sentence type identification, proofreading and spelling or conventions, formal tone

analysis.pattern_summary: Sabrina does fine on content, such as explaining ideas and using passage details, but she loses points on sentence-level tasks that require following an exact instruction (interrogative, appositive, conjunction combining) and on mechanics and proofreading (buy/by, charitys, butterflys, apartment/department, aniamls). Her paragraph responses (Q11) are consistently the weakest or only partly developed item. The G3.6 paragraph was one long run-on sentence with no structure, and the G3.2 paragraph was thin. She also left one item blank (G3.2 Q8) and gave a transformation that changed the sentence type or meaning (G3.4 Q3, G3.5 Q1, Q3). Her scores (69, 87, 80, 76) have not moved steadily upward, which suggests the same sentence-transformation and editing errors keep recurring.
analysis.skill_gaps: appositive phrase construction, sentence-type transformation (declarative to interrogative), combining sentences with conjunctions while keeping all original details, paragraph organization (topic sentence, supporting details, closing sentence), run-on and compound sentence control, spelling and proofreading (homophones, plurals, and typos), elaborating with reasons or text evidence, careful reading of directions, task persistence on short-response items
analysis.alphawrite_vs_test: Sabrina has mastered "Change Sentence To Question," "Write Appositives," and several paragraph skills in AlphaWrite, with one attempt each and no recorded scores. Yet she still misses interrogative, appositive, and paragraph-structure items on the tests, so the skills are not transferring. Mastery may have come too easily, or the activities may not have required the independent, precise application that the tests demand.

mastered_in_alphawrite_not_tests.skill: Identify Topic Sentence And Sequence Details

analysis.pattern_summary: Silver's responses are usually clear and on topic, but they are thin. Across all three tests, grader feedback repeatedly says to "add a reason or example from the story/text." This shows up on one-sentence responses (G3.2 Q8, G3.3 Q10, G3.4 Q6, Q7, Q8) and on paragraph prompts (G3.2 Q11 at 30%, G3.4 Q11 at 60%). Convention errors also keep costing points: spelling ("whiel," "betwen," "ploshon," "impotant," "grope"), homophones ("where/were," "there/their"), and missing words ("good idea name"). Verb precision (G3.4 Q1, "stomped at the flower") and text-evidence use in paragraphs are further weak spots. Scores moved 62% → 82% → 69%, so the G3.3 result did not hold.
analysis.skill_gaps: elaboration with reasons ("because" clauses), text evidence integration, paragraph development and organization (topic sentence, supporting details, concluding sentence), spelling of grade-level words, homophone usage (where/were, there/their), proofreading for omitted words, precise or strong verb choice, character analysis supported by evidence, sentence expansion with when/where/how details, capitalization and punctuation of titles and proper nouns
analysis.alphawrite_vs_test: Silver is marked mastered on "Identify Topic Sentence and Sequence Details" in AlphaWrite, but that skill is recognition, not production. On tests Silver does not write a developed paragraph with supporting evidence, as in G3.2 Q11 (a single sentence) and G3.4 Q11 (details that are loosely connected and not tied to the article's key ideas). The data also covers only 1 attempt with no recorded score, so the mastery signal is weak.
analysis.rushing_impact: No rushing data is provided, but the short answers, the unrevised spelling errors, and the missing words suggest limited proofreading, so rushing may be a moderate contributor, and fixing it would mostly recover the convention errors rather than the elaboration gaps.
analysis.recommended_activities:
- Add a Reason with "Because" (Sentences G3): Silver gives clear claims without reasons in nearly every one-sentence response, and feedback asks for this each time.
- Expand Sentences with Who/What/When/Where/How Details (Sentences G3): the G3.3 Q2 expansion scored 50% and responses are generally sparse.
- Write a Paragraph with Topic Sentence, Evidence, and Conclusion (Paragraphs G3): turns Silver's recognition mastery into production, targeting the one-sentence G3.2 Q11 and the loosely organized G3.4 Q11.
- Use Text Evidence to Support Character Analysis (Writing Brainlift / Reading Response G3): addresses the vague answers on Layla's character and the story's lessons ("be nice to others").
- Choose Stronger Verbs (Sentences G3): directly targets G3.4 Q1, where the replacement verb changed the meaning.
- Proofread: Spelling, Homophones, and Missing Words (Editing G3): a short checklist routine before submitting, aimed at the repeated spelling and word-omission errors.

analysis.pattern_summary: The data shows only two G3 attempts, not the three or more failures in the flag, so earlier attempts may be missing. In the G3.2 attempt (16%, rushed), the student echoed or rephrased the prompt as a question on Q5–Q8 instead of answering it, left Q9 blank, and made conventions errors ("becauce," a comma after *because*, "these event"). The student also could not tighten a sentence by removing the repeated "that day." In G3.4 (78%), the student combined sentences without keeping both ideas or choosing the right connector (used "so" where "but" was needed). The Q11 summary included facts but had awkward, run-on phrasing ("In this text speaks out…"), so the remaining gaps are precise sentence combining, concision, and controlled summary writing.
analysis.skill_gaps: answering questions with complete declarative sentences (not restating the prompt), reading and following prompt directions, choosing conjunctions by logical relationship (but vs. so vs. because), keeping both source ideas when combining sentences, eliminating redundancy and wordiness, comma and punctuation control with conjunctions, spelling of common words, subject-verb and determiner agreement, summary writing with concise sentences, text evidence integration
analysis.alphawrite_vs_test: The student shows every G3 Combining and Paragraphs skill as MASTERED, usually in only 1–2 attempts, yet still misses conjunction choice and sentence-combining on the test, writes run-on summaries, and has trouble with basic responses. This suggests that mastery in AlphaWrite is not transferring to test conditions, such as unscaffolded prompts, text-based tasks, and proofreading under time pressure. Because the best and latest scores are not reported, the depth of mastery cannot be verified.
analysis.rushing_impact: Rushing very likely caused most of the G3.2 failure, since the prompt-echoing, blank Q9, and typos are careless errors rather than missing knowledge, and the student's much higher G3.4 score supports this.

analysis.pattern_summary: Troy's recurring misses are on sentence-level transformation tasks. Appositives were wrong or incomplete on G3.5 (0% and 50%), G3.7 (75%) and G3.9 (50%, where he used a comma splice, "A colony has one leader, she is the queen bee"). Interrogative rewrites also failed (G3.4 Q3 restated the statement for 0%; G3.8 Q4 "Did Jordan asked"). Across single-sentence responses he often gives a claim without the requested reason or example (G3.2 Q6/Q8, G3.4 Q8/Q10, G3.5 Q6 "stood out because they stood out"). Conventions errors also cost points on almost every test: subject-verb agreement, its/their, capitalization, missing end punctuation, "the the", and spelling. Paragraph scores vary from 50% to 90% and are limited mostly by proofreading, not ideas.
analysis.skill_gaps: appositive phrases (construction and identification), converting statements to questions (auxiliary "do/did" with base verb), subject-verb agreement and verb tense, run-ons and comma splices, supporting a claim with a reason or example (avoiding circular reasoning), answering the exact question asked, capitalization and end punctuation, homophones and spelling (their/there, its/their, would), proofreading for repeated words, paragraph elaboration and text-evidence detail
analysis.alphawrite_vs_test: No AlphaWrite data was included, so I can't identify which skills he has mastered there. Within the tests, he handles "because/so" combining and paragraph main ideas reasonably well, but those strengths collapse into errors on appositives, question formation,

analysis.pattern_summary: On G3.2 (51%), Tuf wrote real but underdeveloped responses. He gave fragments instead of complete sentences ("The fans excitement." and "Because it just sonds fun to attent."), merged sentences without keeping the original meaning ("the bear got a goal"), misidentified a declarative sentence as exclamatory, and wrote a one-sentence "paragraph" for the Q11 paragraph prompt. The loop is therefore driven by both skill gaps (complete sentences, sentence combining, sentence types, paragraph elaboration) and disengagement or rushing.
analysis.skill_gaps: complete sentence construction (fragment vs. sentence), sentence combining with conjunctions while preserving meaning, concision/removing redundancy, sentence type identification (declarative vs. exclamatory), paragraph development and elaboration, supporting details from text, spelling/proofreading, test-taking effort and stamina
analysis.alphawrite_vs_test: Tuf shows every listed AlphaWrite skill as MASTERED (Basic Conjunctions, Identify Sentence Type, Write Paragraph From Prompt, Elaborate Paragraphs), yet he failed the same skills on the tests: he missed a sentence type item, wrote a one-sentence response to a paragraph prompt, and produced incomplete combined sentences. analysis.rushing_impact: Rushing very likely had a major effect, especially on G3.6, where the 0% came from placeholder keystrokes rather than demonstrated ability, and it probably depressed G3.2 as well, given the "hhhhhhh" answer and the unfinished, unproofread responses.

analysis.pattern_summary: Vayda's paragraph responses are steady at 60-84% (G3.4 dropped to 60%), but short, single-sentence constructed responses keep scoring 33-50%, and that is what holds her in the loop. She often misses the specific skill a prompt targets: "Sally, went and swam…" is not an appositive, "looked" was never changed to a stronger verb, the G3.1 Q5 dependent clause is still a fragment, and a feelings answer was given where the prompt asked for an action (G3.1 Q7). mastered_in_alphawrite_not_tests.skill: Identify Topic Sentence And Sequence Details

analysis.pattern_summary: Weston's weakest area is sentence-level construction under specific directions. He repeatedly fails to follow the required structure on combining items: "since" was used with reversed meaning, "because" was replaced with "allowing", "so" was used where "and" fits, and "because" was used where an appositive was required. He also loses points on identification and mechanics: he named the verb "Became" as the appositive, wrote "Interrogotive" for a declarative sentence, and left an incomplete "Since…" fragment. His short responses are often incomplete or unsupported because they lack a "because" reason or a specific text detail, and his paragraphs have recurring spelling, possessive, and comma errors. The 51% on G3.2 started the loop, and later scores of 80–89% still left him stuck on 50% items.
analysis.skill_gaps: following the specific conjunction or structure named in the prompt (since/because/appositive), preserving meaning when combining sentences, appositive identification and construction, sentence type identification (declarative vs. interrogative), complete sentences vs. fragments in short responses, supporting opinions with a reason or text detail, paragraph development and closing sentences, spelling and proofreading, possessives and comma usage, changing a statement into a question
analysis.alphawrite_vs_test: All of the AlphaWrite skills are marked mastered, including conjunctions, combining sentences, appositives, changing sentence type, and fragments, yet he still misses these same skills on tests (appositive combining, "because" and "since" combining, sentence-type changes). Mastery appears to reflect recognition in quiz format rather than accurate application in free-text writing, and the missing best/latest scores make the mastery status hard to trust. He does not transfer the skills when he must follow precise directions on his own.
analysis.rushing_impact: Four of the five tests were flagged as rushed, and many errors (ignoring the required word, typos like "Interrogotive," misreading the sentence type, naming "Became" as an appositive) look like carelessness rather than lack of knowledge, so rushing likely contributed substantially to the stalled outcomes.
analysis.recommended_activities:
- Combine Sentences Using Appositives (Production G3): he combined with "because" and misidentified an appositive, so he needs to practice constructing and locating appositives in free-text responses.
- Basic Conjunctions Quiz, retake with free-response items (Combining G3): he misused "since," "because," and "so," and needs to practice meaning-preserving combining with the required conjunction.
- Change Sentence Type (Transformation G3): he misidentified a declarative sentence as interrogative and gave a clumsy question rewrite, so he needs review of sentence types and transformations.
- Fragment Or Sentence (To Sentence G3): his short answers like "Since their favorite team is the 'Bears.'" are fragments, and he has had only 1 attempt.
- Elaborate Paragraphs (Paragraphs G3): he needs practice adding reasons and specific text details, plus a proofreading checklist covering spelling, possessives, and commas, to strengthen his paragraphs and one-sentence responses.

skills.skill: Identify Topic Sentence And Sequence Details

mastered_in_alphawrite_not_tests.skill: Identify Topic Sentence And Sequence Details

analysis.pattern_summary: Willa writes short, mostly on-topic responses but repeatedly leaves out the element the task asks for. Across G3.2–G3.4 she omits a reason or example (Q7 and Q8 on G3.2, Q10 on G3.4), skips a required structure (the conjunction "since" in G3.4 Q2, a stronger verb in G3.4 Q1), and uses fragments or incomplete sentences (G3.4 Q8). She also repeats wording, as in the "that day" redundancy in G3.2 Q1. On the paragraph-length prompts (G3.2 Q11, G3.3 Q11, G3.4 Q11) she either gives a thin answer without text evidence or does not respond at all, and she is increasingly disengaged, with blank answers, "I don't know," and "I don't want to." Scores fell from 64% to 47% to 38% across attempts, which points to eroding effort and persistence on top of the skill gaps.
analysis.skill_gaps: Adding a reason or support in the same sentence, following specific revision directions (subordinating conjunction "since", stronger verbs), concise rewriting and eliminating redundancy, writing complete sentences instead of fragments, using text evidence and details from the passage, developing a full paragraph from an article prompt, explaining what a detail reveals about character or theme, spelling and proofreading, writing stamina and persistence
analysis.alphawrite_vs_test: Willa has mastered every listed AlphaWrite G3 activity, including conjunctions, paragraph elaboration, topic sentences, and writing a paragraph from a prompt, yet she still misses these skills on tests, so the skills are not transferring to timed, independent, text-based responses. The AlphaWrite results show no best or latest percentages (all None) and only 1–2 attempts per activity, so "mastered" may reflect light exposure rather than durable skill, and none of the activities involve responding to an article or passage.
analysis.rushing_impact: The G3.3 test was flagged as rushed and contained two blank responses (Q2 and Q11), so rushing or disengagement likely cost a large share of the 47% score, though the non-rushed G3.4 test still produced 38%, which suggests the skill gaps and motivation matter more than speed alone.
analysis.recommended_activities:
- Combining G3 Basic Conjunctions Quiz (Combining G3): redo with a focus on "since", "because", and "although", because she wrote "so" instead of the required "since" and her attempt count is low. Practice should require her to use the specified word.
- Elaborate Paragraphs (Paragraphs G3): repeat to build the habit of adding reasons and supporting details, since she gave "I would attend…" and "Take pictures and nothing else" without the reason. Use a "because" sentence-stem routine.
- Write Paragraph From Prompt (Paragraphs G3): redo with article-based prompts, because her three paragraph responses lacked evidence or were left blank. She needs scaffolded practice citing details from a passage.
- Turn Outline Into Draft (Paragraphs G3): have her plan with an outline before drafting on article prompts, to lower the barrier to starting and reduce blank or "I don't want to" responses.
- Writing Brainlift sentence-revision practice (Sentences G3): cover stronger verbs, removing repeated words, and rewriting fragments as complete sentences. These match her misses on G3.4 Q1 and Q8 and G3.2 Q1.

analysis.pattern_summary: Wyatt keeps missing the same sentence-level tasks that require a specific named structure. He fails appositives (G3.1 Q1, G3.3 Q3, G3.5 Q4), required conjunctions (G3.1 Q4 and G3.4 Q2, where he used "the reason for that is" and "so" instead of the specified word, and G3.2 Q2, where he used "and" instead of "because"), and sentence-type transformation (G3.4 Q3, where he kept the exclamation mark). His short responses also tend to omit a required part: a reason (G3.2 Q9, G3.4 Q10, G3.1 Q8), an action (G3.1 Q7), or a complete sentence (G3.1 Q6, G3.3 Q7). His longer writing shows run-on and comma-spliced sentences (G3.1 Q11, G3.5 Q7), and G3.5 Q11 copied sentences from the article instead of writing in his own words. Spelling and word-choice errors ("spots," "with" for "will," "Libary") also cost points.
analysis.skill_gaps: appositive phrases, following the specified conjunction or structure in directions, subordinating conjunctions (since, because), changing sentence type (declarative to interrogative), run-on and comma-splice correction, complete sentences with subject and predicate, adding a reason or explanation to a claim, answering the exact question asked (action vs. feeling), paraphrasing instead of copying from the text, paragraph organization and sentence variety, proofreading for spelling and word choice
analysis.alphawrite_vs_test: AlphaWrite shows every G3 skill as mastered after one attempt each, including Basic Conjunctions, Change Sentence Type, and Combine Sentences, yet he still misses these on tests (using "so" instead of "since," leaving an exclamation mark on an interrogative rewrite). The mastery data has no best or latest scores, and one attempt per skill suggests he passed quickly without durable learning, so the skills are not transferring to unprompted test conditions. Appositives do not appear in the mastered list at all, which matches his repeated failures on them.
analysis.rushing_impact: Only G3.1 was flagged as rushed, and rushing probably contributed to its weakest answers (the off-topic Q1 and the incomplete Q6 and Q7), but the same errors recur in later, non-rushed tests, so rushing is not the main cause.
analysis.recommended_activities:
- Combine Sentences Using Appositives (Sentences G3/G4): he failed appositive items on G3.1, G3.3, and G3.5 and added a "by..." phrase or a new idea instead of a noun phrase renaming the noun.
- Subordinating Conjunctions: Since, Because, Although (Sentences G3/G4): he substituted "so," "and," or "the reason for that is" when a specific conjunction was required, so he needs practice following the directed word.
- Change Sentence Type: Declarative to Interrogative (Sentences G3): he left the sentence as a statement with "!" on G3.4 Q3, so he needs repeated practice with word-order changes and question marks.
- Fix Run-ons and Comma Splices (Sentences G3/G4): his G3.1 Q11, G3.5 Q4, and G3.5 Q7 responses join complete thoughts with only commas or "and," and he needs to learn to split or properly connect them.
- Paragraph From Prompt: Paraphrase and Use Evidence in Your Own Words (Paragraphs G3/G4): his G3.5 Q11 copied article sentences, and he needs to practice a claim, a reason, and a detail in his own words, plus a proofreading checklist for spelling and word choice.

analysis.pattern_summary: Xiaochen's errors cluster in sentence-level control rather than idea generation. Across both tests, the student misses on fragment repair (G3.6 Q1 added to the fragment instead of supplying a subject and verb), combining sentences with an appositive (Q3 used "so" instead of an appositive phrase), sentence-type identification (G3.2 Q4 labeled a declarative sentence as exclamatory), and revising for concision and clarity (G3.2 Q1 repeated "that day"). Paragraph responses (Q11) score well at 80-85% but are still marked down for capitalization, spelling ("camles," "pocupines"), possessives, and subject-verb agreement ("Porcupines body has"). Proofreading and mechanics errors persist even on stronger work, which keeps the overall scores from converting into a pass.
analysis.skill_gaps: appositive phrases, sentence combining, fragment repair (supplying subject + predicate), sentence type identification (declarative vs. exclamatory), concision/eliminating redundancy, question transformation and spelling accuracy, capitalization and possessives, subject-verb agreement, proofreading/self-editing
analysis.alphawrite_vs_test: AlphaWrite shows every listed skill, including Fragment Or Sentence and Write Paragraph From Prompt, as MASTERED after a single attempt with no recorded scores (best/latest = None%). Yet the student still fails fragment repair and sentence combining on tests, so the mastery flags likely reflect recognition-level or low-rigor tasks rather than the ability to produce and revise sentences independently.
analysis.rushing_impact: The G3.6 test was flagged as rushed, and its Q1 and Q3 misses (incomplete fragment fix, "so" instead of an appositive) plus the careless spelling and capitalization errors in Q11 suggest rushing moderately contributed, though the same score (84%) as the non-rushed G3.2 test and the repeat G3.2 errors indicate that real skill gaps, not just speed, are the main cause.
analysis.recommended_activities:
- Combine Sentences Using Appositives (Sentences G3/G4): the student replaced the appositive with "so" and needs explicit practice turning a second sentence into a naming phrase set off by commas.
- Fix Fragments by Adding Subject and Verb (Sentences G3): the student's fragment rewrite stayed incomplete, so production-level repair is needed beyond just identifying fragments.
- Identify Sentence Types: Declarative, Interrogative, Exclamatory, Imperative (Sentences G3): the student mislabeled a plain statement as exclamatory and needs practice with purpose and punctuation cues.
- Revise for Concision and Remove Redundancy (Sentences G3): the repeated "that day" shows a need to practice trimming repeated words and phrases.
- Proofread and Edit Your Paragraph checklist routine (Writing Brainlift): spelling, capitalization, possessives, and subject-verb agreement errors keep otherwise strong paragraphs from reaching mastery.
